Abstract: 10

Architected materials derive their properties from the geometric arrangement of their internal 11

structural elements, rather than solely from their chemical composition. They can display 12

remarkable behaviors such as high strength while being lightweight1,2, negative Poisson’s ratios3,4, 13

and shear-normal coupling5,6. However, architected materials so far have either exhibited solid- 14

like1,2 or fluid-like behavior7,8, but not both. Here, we introduce a class of materials that consist of 15

linked particles assembled in three-dimensional domains, forming polycatenated architected 16

materials (PAMs). We propose a general framework for PAMs that translates arbitrary crystalline 17

networks into particles’ concatenations and design particles’ geometry. The resulting materials are 18

cohesive, yet the individual particles retain some kinematic freedom. In response to small external 19

loads, PAMs behave like non-Newtonian fluids, showing both shear-thinning and shear-thickening 20

responses. At larger strains, PAMs behave like solids, showing a nonlinear stress-strain relation, 21

like lattices and foams. These responses are regulated by a jamming transition determined by the 22


<!-- Page 3 -->


2

particles’ arrangement and the direction of loading. PAMs are scalable, showing comparable 23

mechanical responses at both millimeter- and micrometer-scales. However, micro-PAMs can 24

change shape in response to electrostatic charges. PAM’s properties are relevant for developing 25

stimuli-responsive materials, energy-absorbing systems and morphing architectures. 26

Introduction 29

Most architected materials have been designed using rigidly connected truss-1,9, plate-10,11, or 30

shell-based lattices12,13 that derive effective bulk properties from periodically repeating unit 31

cells14,15, or disordered architectures16,17. Depending on the geometry of their interior structure, 32

they exhibit unusual or extreme mechanical properties1,2, such as large reconfigurability18–22, 33

multi-stable responses23,24 and nonlinear elastic deformations25,26. In some realizations, architected 34

materials behave like fluids, like pentamode materials, which present a near-zero shear response7,8. 35

Granular crystals and topologically interlocked panels are a type of architected materials that 36

consist of regular arrays of closely packed elements that interact elastically27,28. They also present 37

rich mechanical properties, such as geometrical hardening29 and nonlinear wave propagation28, 38

which emerge from the geometry of the individual particles, their topological arrangement and the 39

particles’ chemical composition. However, in the absence of boundary confinement, granular 40

crystals are not cohesive, because the particles are not held together by binders, and they offer no 41

resistance in tension. 42

An emergent family of architected materials are topologically interlocked fabrics, consisting 43

of layers of polycatenated particles, like chainmails, which have been shown to support tunable 44


<!-- Page 4 -->


3

stiffness and controllable shape morphing30,31. The concept of polycatenation, rooted in polymer 45

and supramolecular chemistry32–34, refers to the intricate interlinking of molecular structures, 46

typically seen in polycatenated metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) and covalent organic 47

frameworks (COFs)32,33,35,36. The polycatenation of knots and weave-like patterns have been 48

explored through the lens of geometry, introducing a unique facet of reticular chemistry32–34. 49

Here, we integrate the principle of polycatenation into three-dimensional (3D) architected 50

materials that we fabricate at the macro- and micro-scales, to create cohesive arrangements of 51

discrete particles with controllable kinematic degrees of freedom (DOFs). We propose a design 52

strategy to translate continuous graph topologies, such as crystalline lattices37, into their 53

polycatenated counterparts and demonstrate the realization of 3D polycatenated architected 54

materials (PAMs) from selected building blocks. We show how local variations in the particles’ 55

geometry affects the internal DOFs, which, in turn, control the global deformability and effective 56

response of the bulk. Because of the discrete nature of the particle-particle interactions in PAMs, 57

their global mechanical behavior transitions from fluid-like to solid-like, as a function of the 58

applied loading and their response can be preconditioned by repeated loading cycles. We show that 59

PAMs are lightweight and, as opposed to other lattice-based architected materials, they express 60

isotropic responses to different loading conditions. PAMs are resilient to cyclic loading and have 61

tunable energy absorption, with scalable responses that persist at both the macro- and micro-scales. 62

Design approach for PAMs 63

Conversion of continuous graph topologies into PAMs. Traditional lattice structures can be 64

mapped into continuous topological networks that consist of nodes and connections (Fig. 1a). 65

Starting from arbitrary networks, we create periodically entangled toroidal, polygonal, or 66

polyhedral caged particles (hereinafter referred to as ‘particles’) that can be tessellated into PAMs 67


<!-- Page 5 -->


4

at different scales. The process begins by identifying node symmetries in the continuous networks 68

and aligning them with particles that possess these symmetries. These particles interlink with 69

adjacent ones, replicating the original network connections (Figs. 1a-c). Thanks to the enormous 70

database of crystallographic symmetries, topological networks from databases like RCSR37 can be 71

transformed into polycatenated analogs (Extended Data Fig. 1). A single node can be represented 72

using particles with various particle shapes, such as polyhedral wireframes, polygon clusters, or 73

torus clusters (Fig. 1d). Depending on the nature of the constituent units, the topologies of resulting 74

polycatenated architectures exhibit substantial variations (Fig. 1e). 75

Generating 3D PAMs from prescribed particle geometries. A given particle shape can exhibit 76

multiple symmetry axes (Fig. 1f), leading to several potential catenation environments (Figs. 1g- 77

i). By utilizing these catenations singularly or in combination, we can create a variety of PAMs 78

(Figs. 1j-m), each with its own global topology. We employ a tripartite naming scheme, X-n-abc, 79

for easy identification: ‘X’ for the network topology, ‘n’ for the symmetry of local catenation, and 80

‘abc’ for the particle shape, either in full or as an acronym. As an example, the label D-3-tet (Fig. 81

1c) denotes a polycatenated diamond network (D) constituted from tetrahedral wireframes (tet) 82

that interlock corner-to-corner by aligning their 3-fold axes (3). 83

By changing the particles’ shapes within similar symmetries (like from octahedra to 84

cuboctahedra) within a given topology (Extended Data Fig. 2, Supplementary Video 6), we can 85

alter the locking mechanisms (e.g., transitioning from a corner-to-corner linking, as in a J-2-oct to 86

an edge-to-edge interlocking in the J-2-CO), thus varying the DOFs between particles (Extended 87

Data Fig. 2). Reducing the particles’ thickness, thereby decreasing the volume fraction, typically 88

increases the kinematic DOFs between units within the same global topology and the resulting 89

mechanical response of the PAMs. 90

PAM fabrication 91

We fabricated eight representative PAMs, four composed of 2D particles (Figs. 2a-d) and four 92

composed of 3D particles (Figs. 2i-l), using a brittle acrylic polymer using additive manufacturing 93

(see Methods). Each sample was designed to be a cube with side ca. 50 mm (Figs. 2e-h, 2m-p). To 94

maintain 0.1 mm particle-particle separation, wax was used as support materials and later dissolved. 95

Upon removal of the support materials, the PAMs relaxed under gravity and the originally ordered 96

and periodic microstructure became irregular (Figs. 2e-h, 2m-p). Designed and relaxed dimensions 97

are summarized in the Extended Data Table 1. 98

PAMs are characterized by their catenation number (CN), defined as the number of 99

neighboring particles that are catenated with the center one, represented using ball-and-stick 100

models38 (Figs. 2a-d, 2i-l). The same CN can represent multiple local particle arrangements. For 101

example, CN = 4 in a planar arrangement maps to a network with a nbo topology, while CN = 4 102

in a tetrahedral (Td) arrangement maps to a network with a dia topology37. 103

J-2-ring (Fig. 2a) and J-2-sqr (Fig. 2b) were designed to compare the influence of particle 104

geometry while keeping the PAM topology constant. T-2-ring (Fig. 2c) and T-2-hex (Fig. 2d) 105

served as another pair of comparison. J-2-oct (Fig. 2i) and S-4-oct (Fig. 2j) were designed to 106

compare the influence of PAM topology while keeping the particle geometry constant. D-3-tet (Fig. 107

2k) and C-2-TT (Fig. 2l) were designed because they are two results of geometric transformations 108

from T-2 topology – D-3-tet emerge when every two tetrahedral clusters catenated through 3-fold 109

axes are transformed into a pair of tetrahedra; while C-2-TT emerge when every two tetrahedral 110

clusters catenated through 2-fold axes are transformed into a pair of truncated tetrahedra (Extended 111

Data Fig. 2). Notably, J-2-sqr has two stable configurations (Supplementary Video 7): an expanded, 112

stiff configuration (L); and a collapsed, flexible configuration (S). Configuration L can transition 113


<!-- Page 7 -->


6

into S via an auxetic mechanism like the ‘rotating squares behavior’39 (Supplementary Video 8), 114

which can be trained by cyclic application of external loading. To minimize structural randomness, 115

we standardized the maximum permissible particle thicknesses to maintain clearances as 0.1 mm 116

in all designs except for J-2-oct and S-4-oct. 117

Mechanical characterization of PAMs 118

To characterize the mechanical response of PAMs, we conducted compression, shear, and 119

rheology tests under different loading conditions. The mechanical response of PAMs emerges from 120

a complex interplay of interactions across scales, ranging from (i) µm-scale inter-particle contacts, 121

(ii) mm-scale particle deformation (e.g., bending, buckling and fracture), (iii) mesoscale layer-by- 122

layer collapse, and (iv) cm-scale global deformations. Initially, all loadings induce the 123

rearrangement of particles within the available kinematic DOFs and the redistribution of stresses 124

within the volume, without damage to the particles. However, the particles’ rearrangement leads 125

to a bulk deformation of PAMs, which persists even after the removal of the external loads. As the 126

particles reach a jammed state, further spatial reconfiguration becomes untenable. Beyond 127

jamming, continued compressive forces result in particles’ deformation, damage and fracture. 128

Under uniaxial compression (Figs. 3a-g, Supplementary Video 3, Extended Data Fig. 4), all 129

samples exhibit a nonlinear stress-strain behavior with significant loading/unloading hysteresis 130

(energy absorption). This hysteric stress-strain relationship is likely influenced by three distinct 131

mechanisms: (i) the rearrangement of catenated particles, (ii) the presence of friction, and (iii) at 132

larger strains, particle deformation and damage. 133

Repeated loading and unloading cause PAMs to develop a permanent residual strain. Under 134

cyclic compression at lower strains, PAMs show a reduced peak stress and a hysteretic response 135


<!-- Page 8 -->


7

with a progressively smaller area, leading to less energy being dissipated in each cycle (Extended 136

Data Fig. 4). Most of this reduction happens within the first few cycles, after which the PAMs 137

stabilize into a steady-state response. This initial drop in energy dissipation, known as 138

preconditioning, is a common characteristic of many rubbery40 and biological41 materials. Under 139

cyclic compression with progressively increasing strain (from 10% to 50%), the material continues 140

to follow the primary loading path until extensive damage occurs, as long as the strain in each 141

cycle exceeds the maximum strain of the previous cycle (Fig. 3a-g). These observations mirror the 142

Mullins effect seen in certain rubbers44. 143

In granular systems, particles’ shape significantly affects macroscopic mechanical 144

properties30,42, this can also be observed in PAMs. T-2-ring and T-2-hex exhibit comparatively 145

lower stiffness and can withstand maximum strain without damage to their constituent units (Figs. 146

3a,b), unlike PAMs composed of polyhedral particles (Figs. 3c,f,g). This discrepancy can be 147

attributed to the fact that jamming in polyhedron-based PAMs occurred at lower strain values than 148

in 2D polygons or rings (Figs. 3a-g). Additionally, the larger number of kinematic DOFs and the 149

coupled deformation modes of rings and hexagonal particles resulted in lower overall PAM’s 150

stiffness. This phenomenon is reminiscent of powders, where sphere-like particles (analogous to 151

PAMs composed of polyhedral particles) are found to exhibit higher compressive strength and 152

elastic modulus, as compared to flake-like particles (analogous to T-2-ring and T-2-hex)43. PAMs 153

with fewer kinematic DOFs, like J-2-ring, J-2-sqr, in addition to structures composed of polyhedral 154

particles, displayed higher stiffness (Figs. 3d,e,h). Therefore, PAMs can be designed to present 155

higher stiffness by (i) increasing the edge numbers of particles, or (ii) disrupting kinematic DOFs 156

among particles. 157

Unlike other architected materials, PAMs exhibit a notable ability to adjust their interparticle 158

arrangements in response to external loads, a characteristic also found in granular systems. This 159

particles’ rearrangement leads to two mechanical regimes, which appear under all deformation 160

modes: (i) a fluid-like response, with a vanishing shear modulus, linked to relative particles’ 161

motion; and (ii) a solid-like response, characterized by particles’ deformation, beyond the jamming 162

transition. To describe the fluid-like mechanical response, we conducted shear and rheology tests 163

on J-2-ring and T-2-ring samples (Figs. 4a,b). These PAMs were selected because they are 164

composed of toroidal particles, which have greater kinematic DOFs. To control testing conditions, 165

we fabricated samples that incorporated top and bottom gripping plates (Figs. 4a,b; Extended Data 166

*Fig. 3). 167*

Under shear loads, both J-2-ring and T-2-ring samples demonstrated a plateau region with 168

force values close to zero, indicative of a fluid-like behavior (Figs. 4c,f, Supplementary Video 3). 169

Beyond a critical strain, such plateau then transitioned to a quasi-linear elastic region, typical of 170

solid-like behavior. This transition can be correlated to the reduced DOFs between rings, which 171

jam under external tensile, compressive or shear loads. The fluid-like and solid-like regimes can 172

be programmed by designing the catenation topologies and particle geometries. 173

To further understand this fluid-solid duality, we characterized the rheological properties of 174

cylindrical shaped PAM samples (Fig. 4b, Supplementary Video 4). In oscillatory amplitude sweep 175

experiments (Figs. 4d,g), the J-2-ring and T-2-ring samples initially displayed a decrease in storage 176

modulus (G’), loss modulus (G’’), and complex viscosity (η*) with increasing torsional strain. 177

Upon reaching the critical jamming strain observed in simple shear tests, all three parameters begin 178

to increase. This behavior parallels observations in certain shear thickening fluids. However, shear 179

thickening fluids initially undergo only a minimal shear thinning phase that results in a small 180


<!-- Page 10 -->


9

reduction of viscosity44. In contrast, PAMs show a much more significant reduction in viscosity, 181

which decreases by several orders of magnitude (Figs. 4d,g). 182

In the frequency sweep experiments (Figs. 4e,h), both J-2-ring and T-2-ring samples exhibited 183

an unusual inflection in viscosity at high angular frequency. When subjected to torsional strains 184

below their respective jamming transition thresholds, a notable transition from shear-thinning to 185

shear-thickening was observed with increasing oscillation angular frequency. This transition is 186

likely due to the inertia effects of particles under high-frequency oscillation conditions. 187

To understand this unusual frequency-dependent thinning-to-thickening transition, we 188

modeled the response of PAMs using the level-set discrete element method (LS-DEM)45,46. We 189

focus on modeling the rheological experiments, and the inflection of η* with increasing angular 190

frequency. Since the mechanical deformation of each particle is minimal compared to the 191

translation observed in their rigid body motion (e.g., rearrangement) in the experiments, we model 192

the rings as rigid particles. LS-DEM can model the contact dynamics among granular particles of 193

arbitrary shapes, and it has been applied to model systems made of 3D-printed particles30,47. Here, 194

we use LS-DEM to model sweep experiments for both J-2-ring and T-2-ring samples. We construct 195

digital twins, replicating the ring’s shape, density, size, spatial arrangement, as well as the total 196

number of rings in each respective sample. 197

All simulations qualitatively capture the inflection of η* observed in experiments (compare 198

Figs. 4i,k with Figs. 4e,h). Our simulations also agree with experiments in that the value of η* at 199

the inflection point is smaller for the J-2-ring sample compared to the that for the T-2-sample. 200

However, the simulations overestimate the angular frequency at which the inflection of η* happens. 201

This mismatch could be due to imprecisions in the experimental particle geometry, contacts’ 202

imperfections and the presence of friction, which are not included in our models. These 203


<!-- Page 11 -->


10

discrepancies can also lead to considerable differences in the initial sample’s packing structure in 204

the relaxed configuration in experiments and simulations, which can shift the angular frequency at 205

which the inflection of η* happens. Nevertheless, our simulations provide particle-scale details that 206

allow us to better understand the mechanisms underpinning this thinning-to-thickening transition. 207

More specifically, from the point view of the rheophysics of dense granular materials48–50, η* takes 208

contribution from two components: a “contact” component (which corresponds to percolating 209

force chains in the statics of granular media, used often in the soil mechanics community), and a 210

“fluctuation” component (which corresponds to the degree of turbulency of granular flow, used 211

often in the fluid mechanics community). 212

In our experiments, as the excitation frequency increases, it is expected that both samples 213

experience a transition from a contact-dominant (or “quasi-static”) regime to a fluctuation- 214

dominant (or “inertia”) regime. As such, the initial decrease of η* can be understood as the decrease 215

of contact (due to stronger centrifugal effects) in the contact-dominant regime, while the later 216

increase of η* can be understood as the increased degree of “turbulency” (due to a faster external 217

excitations) in the fluctuation-dominant regime. This concept is confirmed by looking at Fig. 4j, 218

which shows, for the simulation of the J-2 ring sample, the variation of the average contact number 219

per particle, and of the normalized average particle velocity fluctuation (computed as the square 220

root of granular temperature48, see Methods for our calculation procedure), as functions of the 221

angular frequency. As the angular frequency increases, the average contact number per particle 222

decreases while the particle velocity fluctuation increases. In particular, the latter shows a much 223

rapid increase rate once crossing the inflection point of η*, which suggests the transition from the 224

contact-dominant regime to the fluctuation-dominant regime. A similar observation can be made 225

for the T-2 ring sample, by looking at Fig. 4l and comparing it to Fig. 4j. 226

Programmable critical jamming strains 227

We study the role of particle geometry and particle’s linking topology in the jamming 228

transition in PAMs. The local catenation topologies in PAMs play a pivotal role in defining their 229

mesoscale (e.g., cell-to-cell, layer-by-layer) DOFs, which in turn dictates the critical strain for 230

jamming (𝜀𝜀𝑐𝑐 ∗: critical compressive jamming strain; 𝛾𝛾𝑠𝑠 ∗: critical shear jamming strain). For instance, 231

J-2-ring PAMs show a significantly higher 𝛾𝛾𝑠𝑠 ∗ as compared to T-2-ring PAMs, whereas T-2-ring 232

exhibits a higher 𝜀𝜀𝑐𝑐 ∗ relative to J-2-ring. In J-2-ring PAMs, shear loading induces a coordinated 233

rearrangement of particles, thereby amplifying 𝛾𝛾𝑠𝑠 ∗ (Fig. 5a). During this process, rings oriented 234

parallel to the shearing direction maintain their orientations, while those perpendicular to the 235

shearing direction rotate in a coordinated manner, facilitating a greater 𝛾𝛾𝑠𝑠 ∗ . However, under 236

compression or tension, the rings’ inability to adjust their positions – restricted by limited DOFs 237

from neighboring particles – results in a reduced 𝜀𝜀𝑐𝑐 ∗. In contrast, T-2-ring PAMs rely on a ‘scissor’ 238

mechanism (Fig. 5c): Upon compressive loading, all rings adjust their orientations coordinatively, 239

which allows for a larger 𝜀𝜀𝑐𝑐 ∗. 240

In addition to the choice of catenation topology, the thickness, d, of the torus significantly 241

influences the jamming transition in PAMs (Fig. 5d). A decrease in d generally correlates with an 242

increased DOF in PAMs. To elucidate this relationship, we fabricated a series of J-2-ring and T-2- 243

ring PAMs with constant ring diameters (D) but varied d. We measured the critical jamming strain 244

under both shear (𝛾𝛾𝑠𝑠 ∗) and compressive (𝜀𝜀𝑐𝑐 ∗) loading conditions as a function of thickness d (Fig. 245

5b). Regardless of the catenation topology, reductions in d are associated with increases in both 𝛾𝛾𝑠𝑠 ∗ 246

and 𝜀𝜀𝑐𝑐 ∗. Furthermore, we observed that catenation topology significantly impacts the predominant 247

deformation modes. For instance, the 𝛾𝛾𝑠𝑠 ∗ for J-2-ring PAM (Fig. 5d), which exhibit the largest d/D 248

ratio and therefore the lowest DOF, is higher compared to T-2-ring PAMs (Fig. 5o), which have a 249

much lower d/D ratio. 250

Length-scale dependence and electrostatic reconfiguration of µ-PAMs 251

The deformability of PAMs is primarily influenced by their particle geometries, which can 252

be scaled across several particles’ dimensions. This suggests that the mechanical responses of 253

PAMs should remain consistent across scales (i.e., macroscopic to microscopic). To validate this 254

hypothesis, we fabricate PAMs using multiphoton lithography and oxygen plasma etching (see 255

Methods). Upon completion of the fabrication and activation process—where plasma etching 256

removes thin support materials required during fabrication – the µ-PAMs demonstrated a 257

gravitational relaxation analogous to that observed in their macroscopic counterparts (Extended 258

Data Fig. 10). We designed a series of C-2-TT PAMs (as in Fig. 3c) varying their volume fractions, 259

by changing the beam thicknesses of the particles. Following an increasing order of beam thickness, 260

we label the PAMs as I, II, and III (Extended Data Fig. 6). The same PAMs were fabricated at both 261

macroscale (Ω_I, Ω_II, Ω_III) and microscale (µ_I, µ_II, µ_III), scaling them by a factor of 60 in 262

all dimensions (i.e., sample side lengths: 24 mm and 400 µm). Due to the differences in fabrication 263

methods, we used slightly different acrylic polymers (Material properties in Methods) for the 264

macro- and micro-scale samples. Nevertheless, we found qualitative agreement between the 265

mechanical responses of PAMs across scales (Figs. 6a-c). The energy absorption capacities (U) of 266

all C-2-TT PAMs were calculated by integrating the areas under the stress-strain curves. Our 267

experiments reveal that scale factors (Uµ/ UΩ) among all I, II, III designs to be near constant of 268

12.76±0.53 (Fig. 6a). To test if µ-PAMs also possess fluid-like properties, we tessellated J-2-ring 269

µ-PAM voxels to form various geometries: a side-anchored cube (Fig. 6d), a point-anchored cube 270

(Fig. 6e), a bottom-anchored numeral ‘1’ (Fig. 6f), and a bottom-anchored letter ‘T’ (Fig. 6g). 271

One defining difference between micro-scale and macro-scale PAMs is their dramatically 272

different surface-to-volume ratio (~3,600 times larger in the µ-PAM samples). Such discrepancy 273

can be exploited to observe the role of surface forces in the global deformation of PAMs. To test 274

this hypothesis, we electroplated each µ-PAM sample with a thin layer of copper, approximately 275

300 nm in thickness, to provide electrical conductivity. We then positioned the samples atop a Van 276

de Graaff generator with direct electrical contact (Extended Data Fig. 10). As electrostatic charge 277

accumulated, the individual rings within the µ-PAMs began to repel each other, due to increased 278

electrostatic repulsion. This electrostatic interaction prompted the µ-PAMs to both expand outward 279

in all directions due to inter-ring repulsion and elongate upwards due to repulsion between the µ- 280

PAMs and the substrate, transforming each initially relaxed structure into a structurally deployed 281

state (Figs. 6d-g, Supplementary Video 6). The transition between the natural, compact state and 282

the electrified, deployed state was fast (<1 s, Supplementary Video 9) and completely reversible. 283

This suggests that µ-PAMs driven by electrostatic forces can be engineered as responsive elements 284

in remotely actuated materials, for micro-scale devices and smart material systems. 285

Discussions 286

Our work introduces PAMs as a novel class of architected materials, distinguished by their 287

ability to exhibit both fluid-like and solid-like behaviors regulated by a jamming transition, which 288

we demonstrate both at the macro- and micro-scales. By mapping discrete, topologically 289

interlocked particles onto 3D crystalline networks, PAMs achieve programmable mechanical 290

responses that can be precisely controlled by the particles’ geometry and arrangement. The solid- 291

fluid duality of PAMs opens new frontiers in the design of architected materials. Their nonlinear 292

elastic response in the jammed state, coupled with non-Newtonian shear-thinning and shear- 293

thickening behaviors in the unjammed state, provides a versatile mechanical platform for 294


<!-- Page 15 -->


14

applications requiring adaptive stiffness and energy dissipation. This is particularly relevant for 295

stimuli-responsive materials, soft robotics, and morphing architectures. By leveraging the 296

principles of polycatenation and topology, this work lays the foundation for creating architected 297

materials with unprecedented control over mechanical properties and responsiveness. 298

Methods: 489

Materials and Fabrication of Macroscopic PAMs 490

PAM samples were fabricated using additive manufacturing from 3D Systems employing the 491 Multi Jet Fusion fabrication process, sourced from a commercial 3D printing service (Shapeways). 492 Materials used in this study are Visijet M3, M2R-Clear, and M2R-TN. All mechanical tests were 493 conducted using PAMs fabricated using Visijet M3. Visijet M3 has a density of 1.02 g/cm3, a 494 tensile modulus of 1463 MPa, and a tensile strength of 42.4 MPa51. Upon receiving the samples, 495 some had remaining supporting wax materials, which could (i) alter the particle geometries and (ii) 496 limit particles’ DOFs. These wax materials can be selectively dissolved by soaking the samples in 497 isopropanol solution for 2 min at a temperature between 40 and 60 °C. All PAM samples were 498 manually checked to ensure no remaining particle agglutination before mechanical 499 characterizations. To test PAM samples under shear loading (in simple shear and rheology tests), 500 we incorporated two solid gripping plates in the sample’s design and fabrication (Extended Data 501 Fig. 3). The plates partially overlapped with the particles at the top and bottom surfaces and were 502 used to mount the samples to the loading grips and distribute the load uniformly across all particles 503 on the surfaces. 504

Quasi-static Compression and Shear Tests 505

Quasi-static uniaxial compression and simple shear experiments were conducted using an 506 Instron ElectroPuls E3000 universal testing machine. This testing machine was equipped with an 507 ATI Mini85 multi-axial Force/Torque sensor capable of measuring both force and torque along 508 three mutually perpendicular axes. The load cell’s capacity was 1.9 kN and 3.8 kN for force 509 measurements in the X, Y, and Z directions respectively, and 80 Nm for torque measurement along 510 all three axes. For the quasi-static compression trials, cubic specimens were carefully positioned 511 between the compression platens. The orientation ensured that the centerline of the specimen was 512 aligned with the centerline of the load cell. To mount the shear test specimens in the Instron 513 machine, a pair of custom-designed mounting plates was affixed to the solid gripping plates (3D- 514 printed alongside the specimen). The specimens were oriented such that the solid gripping plates 515 aligned with the sides of the specimen. Each mounting plate was subsequently connected to the 516 corresponding upper and lower parts of the tensile grip in the Instron. This modification 517 transformed the uniaxial tensile/compression test apparatus into a configuration suitable for simple 518 shear testing. The force-displacement responses of all specimens were recorded during quasi-static 519 compression tests, at a displacement-controlled loading rate of 0.1/s, to maintain experimental 520 consistency. In the compression tests, a series of multiple compression cycles were performed on 521 a single specimen, each with a varying maximum loading strain spanning from 10% to 50%. Due 522 to the inherently stochastic nature of PAMs, their dimensions exhibited variability in each instance, 523 influenced by random internal arrangement patterns. Thus, dimensions of relaxed PAMs under 524 gravity were measured multiple times, across various regions. The resultant average measurements 525 were then utilized to compute effective stress and strain, accounting for this variability. 526

Rheology Tests 527

The dynamic oscillatory rheological tests were performed using a torque-controlled Discovery 528 HR20 Hybrid Rheometer, from TA Instruments which has axial force and torque limits of 50 N 529 and 0.2 Nm with sensitivities at 0.005 N and 10-10 Nm, respectively. The experiment was carried 530


<!-- Page 26 -->


25

out using a 40 mm diameter parallel plate tool, maintaining a constant temperature of 25 °C and a 531 frequency of 0.5 Hz, with the torsional strain ranging from 10-6 % to 100%. Cylindrical specimens 532 of original height and diameter of 40 mm were employed. These specimens were designed with 533 thin solid components at both ends, strategically incorporated to ensure steadfast attachment to the 534 rheometer and prevent any slippage. To achieve this secure attachment, thin, robust double-sided 535 adhesive tapes were utilized. Torsional rotation was applied to the specimen through the upper 536 parallel plate, while the bottom side remained securely fixed. Data acquisition was facilitated using 537 the TRIOS software. Data points lying within the strain range of 10-6 % to 10-3 %, were subjected 538 to noise interference and were deliberately excluded from the study. 539

The inter-particle 543 friction for the J-2-ring was set as 0.25, same as in the previous work30. The inter-particle friction 544 for the T-2-ring sample was increased to 0.5, to partially account for the noticeable surface 545 roughness of the 3D-printed ring particles. 546

Fabrication and Characterization of Microscopic PAMs 598

The µ-PAM samples were fabricated by two-photon lithography using a commercial 3D 599 printer (Nanoscribe GT2) and a commercial resin (Nanoscribe IP-S). The smaller samples used in 600 micro-mechanical compression experiments were printed as designed, without adding additional 601 mechanical supports. The larger samples used in electrostatic deployment experiments were 602


<!-- Page 28 -->


27

printed by stitching multiple segments sequentially due to the limited field of view of the 25X 603 objective used for two-photon lithography. To prevent drifting issues of the interlocked but 604 unsupported structures due to the prolonged printing time for larger µ-PAM structures, we 605 incorporated additional support structures (body-centered cubic lattices with lateral beam 606 thickness of 500 nm) that overlapped with the µ-PAM lattices in the CAD design. The combined 607 geometry was printed simultaneously so that the body-centered cubic scaffold provided additional 608 support and confinement of the PAM during the printing process. The as-printed samples were 609 immersed in propylene glycol methyl ether acetate (Sigma-Aldrich) for 1hr and then in isopropanol 610 for 1hr to rinse off the remaining uncured liquid resin. The cleaned samples were dried in air. # Granular metamaterials with dynamic bond reconfiguration

**Authors:** Zhiqiang Meng; Hujie Yan; Yifan Wang

**Affiliations:** 1School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Nanyang Technological University, 50 Nanyang Avenue, Singapore 639798, Singapore. | 2Department of Mechanical and Civil Engineering, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA.

## Abstract

Biological materials dynamically reconfigure their underlying structures in response to stimuli, achieving adaptability and multifunctionality. Conversely, mechanical metamaterials have fixed interunit connections that restrict adaptability and reconfiguration. This study introduces granular metamaterials composed of discrete bimaterial structured particles that transition between assembled and unassembled states through mechanical compression and thermal stimuli. These materials enable dynamic bond reconfiguration, allowing reversible bond breaking and formation, similar to natural systems. Leveraging their discrete nature, these materials can adaptively reconfigure their shape and respond dynamically to varying conditions. Our investigations reveal that these granular metamaterials can substantially alter their mechanical properties, like compression, shearing, and bending, offering tunable mechanical characteristics across different states. Furthermore, they exhibit collective behaviors like directional movement, object capture, transportation, and gap crossing, showcasing their potential for reprogrammable functionalities. This work highlights the dynamic reconfigurability and robust adaptability of granular metamaterials, expanding their potential in responsive architecture and autonomous robotics.

## Abstract

Granular metamaterials use bond formation and breaking for shape reconfiguration, tunable properties, and collective motion.

## INTRODUCTION

Biological materials and organisms showcase remarkable abilities to reconfigure their internal structures in response to various stimuli dynamically. Examples include the reconfigurable protein assemblies (1) and the fusion and fission capabilities of cell membranes (2). A more common example is water molecules forming hydrogen bonds to create a solid crystalline structure when freezing into ice and dissociating these bonds upon melting (3). These capabilities substantially enhance their adaptability and functionality in diverse environments. Similarly, synthetic polymer materials with dynamic bonding interactions, such as dynamic covalent polymers and vitrimers, exhibit unique properties, including self-healing and recyclability (4, 5). These transitions hinge on the dynamic formation and breaking of intermolecular bonds.

In contrast, mechanical metamaterials are solids with well-defined lattice structures that often surpass their constituent materials (6, 7) in properties like the Poisson’s ratio (8–10), stiffness (11–15), energy absorption capacity (16–18), fracture resistance (19, 20), and shape transformation (21–24). However, unlike biological and polymeric materials with dynamic bond reconfigurations, these mechanical metamaterials tend to maintain structural integrity postfabrication and cannot alter their internal connections in response to external stimuli, limiting their potential for reconfigurability and adaptability. Recent advances, such as the implementation of structured gears with variable stiffness, have enabled reconfigurable mechanical properties through relative gear rotation (25). Furthermore, topological modifications in gear arrangements have been shown to effectively control local flexibility and global stability (26). Nevertheless, once fabricated, these mechanical metamaterials lack the ability to be disassembled upon external stimuli and reconfigured into other topological arrangements. This prompts a fundamental question: Can mechanical metamaterials be endowed with dynamic bond reconfigurability akin to biological and polymeric materials, achieving structural reconfigurability and multifunctionality?

Granular materials, composed of discrete particles, inherently exhibit complex phenomena such as granular flows and jamming transition, which arise from the collective interactions of individual particles (27–29). Their discrete nature combined with aggregability leads to unlimited possibilities in their internal structural configurations, which hold great potential for addressing the aforementioned challenge. Particularly, the rapidly growing field of granular metamaterials endeavors to tailor the properties of granular materials by designing discrete building blocks (30). This is achieved by creating particles with complex shapes (31–34), entanglement mechanisms (35, 36), auxetic behaviors (37, 38), multistability (39–41), and diverse contact interactions (42, 43). Their broad design space and unique properties enable the transition between liquid-like states upon bond breaking and solid-like states after bond formation. For granular metamaterials featuring assembly from discrete particles, various physical mechanisms can be used. For example, nanoparticles can be assembled into crystalline structures through self-assembly or directed assembly (44, 45), and nonconvex particles can form load-bearing structures through topological interlocking mechanisms (30, 46, 47). Nevertheless, the assembly of existing granular materials into functional structures still requires confinement mechanisms such as tensioned ropes (42, 48), bags with negative pressures (33, 46), liquid bridges between particles (49), or molecular interactions (44). These existing methods require additional components or external stresses to maintain the assembled structure, which presents notable challenges for reprogramming after assembly, especially for the need for structure reconfiguration under environmental stimuli such as temperature. The use of bistability within particles offers a promising solution, providing reconfigurability and transition between stable states (50–52).

Once dynamic bond reconfiguration is achieved, fascinating adaptation and functionality may emerge in diverse environments (53). In nature, animals like fire ants and California blackworms form entangled swarms via mechanical interlocking, enabling adaptive self-assembly and reorganization by allowing each member to attach to and detach from its neighbors (54–57). Mimicking such behaviors, robot or material collectives have been developed to interact with their environment through reconfiguration (58–66). For example, contact-based macroscale robot collectives (59, 60) can adjust their shape, function, locomotion mode, and mechanical properties. Kilobot collectives (61, 62) can use programmed interactions to create different formations and reconfigure object manipulation based on global signal inputs. Furthermore, externally driven collectives can be manipulated by magnetic fields (63, 64), heat (65), light (66), acoustics (58), or other global stimuli. By embedding such a collective behavior into granular metamaterials, multifunctionality can be achieved by harnessing both the intrinsic properties of discrete individual particles and the collective dynamic or structural properties of assembled granular materials.

In this research, to create dynamically reconfigurable metamaterials that exhibit a collective behavior, we developed granular metamaterials consisting of bimaterial structured particles capable of bond reconfiguration through thermal and mechanical stimuli. By mechanically compressing initially discrete particles into contact, we facilitated the formation of bistable interlocks (i.e., bond formation), enabling the transition from an unassembled (liquid-like) state to an assembled (solid-like) state. Subsequent heating of the assembled granular metamaterials enables bond breaking between particles, reverting them to a flowing liquid (disassembled) state. Unlike most previous mechanical metamaterials, our approach overcomes the limitation of fixed unit cell connections, enabling rearrangement of their structures. We thoroughly investigated the tunable mechanical properties of these materials in different states. Furthermore, by introducing active particles and leveraging their structural reconfigurability, we demonstrated the collective functionalities of granular metamaterials, including directional movement, object capture, transportation, and gap crossing. This research opens a route for developing advanced materials combining dynamic reconfigurability with multifunctional capabilities, potentially transforming applications in areas such as soft robotics, adaptive structures, and intelligent materials.

## RESULTS

### Design of bond-reconfigurable granular metamaterials

Temperature-responsive bimaterial structures play a substantial role in regulating the mechanical properties of mechanical metamaterials, such as bistability and stiffness modulation (14, 23, 67–69). Drawing inspiration from this, we used multimaterial printing technology to construct bimaterial structured particles (Fig. 1A) endowed with bond-reconfigurable capabilities. The particle comprises insertion pins (IPs) and receiving clips (RCs), which are staggered in arrangement. As shown in Fig. 1A and fig. S3, each IP consists of a support rod and an elliptical head fabricated from polylactic acid (PLA; depicted in green). Conversely, the RC is constructed from two triangular blocks, each featuring a groove, and is made of the elastic thermoplastic polyurethane (TPU; depicted in white). The RC is interconnected with the IP through a ligament fabricated from TPU (see fig. S3 for details). Here, we define n = 8 to indicate that each particle is composed of eight IPs and eight RCs; configurations with n = 9 and n = 10 are also available (see the Supplementary Materials and fig. S4 for details).

Figure 1B illustrates the compression-induced bond formation between two freely rotatable particles. Under compression, the IP of one particle initiates contact with the RC of another (Fig. 1B, ii). The RC, constructed from the more flexible TPU, deforms under the pressure exerted by the IP, which is composed of the stiffer PLA. This contact modulates the relative positioning of the particles. As compression progresses, the RC transforms to its second stable deformed configuration (Fig. 1B, iii). In this configuration, the grooves on the RC effectively engage with the elliptical head on the IP to achieve locking (see the right inset in Fig. 1B), thus facilitating the formation of a mechanical bond between the particles (see movie S1 for the whole process). The interlock remains stable due to the bistability of the RC.

Figure 1C demonstrates the heat-induced bond breaking process of two interlocked particles captured through infrared thermography. Initially, a heat gun is used to heat the system, with an increase in temperature indicated by the color brightening (Fig. 1C, i to iii). This rise in temperature leads to the softening of the IPs, reducing the constraint on the RC and causing a transition from a bistable to a monostable state. Subsequently, the RC returns to its initial unfolded state, and the interlock between the two particles is disengaged (Fig. 1C, iii to vi). This process releases elastic energy from the bistable structure, causing the two particles to spring apart and generate a separating velocity, corresponding to the bond breaking (see movie S2 for the whole process).

Using this bond-reconfigurable characteristic of the particles, Fig. 1D depicts the bond formation and breaking process in our proposed granular metamaterials. Initially, randomly positioned discrete particles are subjected to external compressive loads (Fig. 1D, left). The particles spontaneously adjust their relative positions due to geometry constraints, enabling the IPs and RCs within the particles to align roughly. The IPs and RCs lock together as compression continues, forming bonds within the granular metamaterial (Fig. 1D, middle). Consequently, the particles transition from an unassembled, discrete flowing state to an assembled rigid state, akin to the phase transition from a liquid to a solid. Subsequently, heating the assembled granular metamaterial causes the internal bonds to break, resulting in disassembly into discrete particles (Fig. 1D, right). This process mimics a melting transition from a solid state to a liquid state. To showcase the substantially different mechanical properties in unassembled and assembled states, several examples are presented in Fig. 1E. In the unassembled state (Fig. 1E, left), the particles in the container flow like a liquid and can be poured out. In contrast, in the assembled state, the metamaterial exhibits mechanical characteristics typical of solid materials, including rigidity under compression, bending, shearing, and tension (Fig. 1E, right).

Furthermore, we developed an active particle with locomotive abilities to enable collective motions in granular metamaterials. As shown in Fig. 1F, this particle enhances the bimaterial structured particle by incorporating a drive module with a remote control. The wheel at the bottom of the particle (Fig. 1F, right) elevates the particle, creating an angle θ with the ground. Driven by a motor, the wheel propels the particle to move. A single active particle is limited to circular motion and cannot achieve directional movement (see movie S7). In contrast, the assembled granular metamaterial, consisting of two active particles and eight passive particles (Fig. 1G), is capable of collective directional movement and can navigate around obstacles (see movie S7).

### Mechanical characterization and analysis of the reconfigurable bond

To quantitatively investigate the mechanism of bond formation and bond breaking between particles, we conducted theoretical analysis, experimental tests, and finite element analysis (FEA), as illustrated in Fig. 2 and figs. S5 to S18. For compression-induced bond formation, it is essential to investigate the deformation and mechanical response during compression (Fig. 2, A to C, and movie S1). Figure 2A shows the experimentally measured force-displacement response of two particles capable of relative rotation under compression, with parameters l = 1.0 mm , t 0 = 0.5 mm , L = 8 mm , R = 22 mm , θ 0 = 55 ° , and n = 8 (see the Supplementary Material and figs. S3 and S4). Results show that varying initial relative positions of the two particles lead to distinctly different mechanical responses during compression. When the IP (red dashed line in the top-left inset in Fig. 2A) forms an angle of φ = 22.5 ° with the normal of another particle’s RC (black dashed line), a larger force is required to induce a snap-through and form a bond. The initial angle φ between the IP and RC reduces to zero upon bond formation, facilitated by their sliding contact (see fig. S12 for details). In another case, when the initial angle between the IP and RC is 0 ° (see Fig. 2A, bottom-right inset), less force is needed to enable bond formation. When the free rotation of particles is restricted by surrounding boundaries, their assembly process can be influenced. Under such constrained conditions, a dual interlocking set can still form, enabling the assembly to proceed (see the Supplementary Materials and fig. S17). Nonetheless, it is essential to note that successful interlocking between certain particles may not be achievable in certain extreme cases of confinement. However, even in such cases, the presence of multiple neighboring particles typically ensures that the overall structure remains stable and functional despite localized assembly defects. In addition, as the symmetry of the particle increases, indicated by larger n values, the number of IPs and RCs also increases. This potentially simplifies the assembly process by offering more bonding opportunities, although it requires higher fabrication precision due to the smaller size of RCs and IPs.

To better understand the bistability of RC, we established a theoretical model (Fig. 2B). In this model, the RC is represented as two rigid triangular plates. The ligaments connecting the RC to the IP are modeled as a torsion spring with a stiffness of K t 1 , and the interconnecting ligament between plates is modeled using a combination of three linear springs (Fig. 2B, bottom): Stretching or compression is captured by a spring with stiffness K l ; shearing is described by a spring with stiffness K s ; and bending is modeled by a torsional spring with stiffness K t 2 . Under these assumptions, the stability of RC in the bimaterial structured particle can be theoretically predicted as functions of θ 0 and l / L (see the Supplementary Materials and figs. S6 and S7 for details). In the case of bistability, the potential energy curve exhibits both a local maximum W max and a local minimum W min . We defined factor η as ( W max − W min ) / W max (see insets in Fig. 2C and fig. S8) to quantify the relative difference between these local extremum points. However, in the case of monostability, the potential energy curve is monotonically increasing and does not exhibit both a local maximum and a local minimum. Therefore, η is not defined for monostability. The contour plot of η in the θ 0 ~ l / L space is shown in Fig. 2C, in which the green solid line represents the boundary between monostability and bistability. The bottom-left (purple) region represents bistable states, and the top-right (gray) region represents monostable states. The model was verified against experimental measurements (symbols in Fig. 2C) and then adopted for the design of bistable bimaterial structured particles.

For heat-induced bond breaking, it is essential to understand the changes in the bond properties as a result of increasing in temperature (Fig. 2, D to F). The IPs and RCs are made of PLA and TPU, respectively. As characterized by dynamic mechanical analysis (DMA) (see the Supplementary Materials and fig. S2), PLA exhibits a relatively high modulus at room temperature ( E PLA 25 ≈ 2.3 GPa at 25°C), which drops substantially when heated above its glass transition temperature, T g ( E PLA 70 ≈ 5.33 MPa at 70°C). In contrast, TPU has a relatively constant modulus when the temperature increases from 25° to 70°C. FEA results of compressing and heating two particles (Fig. 2, E and F; see movie S2) reveal the transition from bistability to monostability induced by increasing temperature. In the locked state (i) (Fig. 2E, left), the end of the IP made of PLA experiences notable stress, resulting in bistability as depicted by the pink curve in Fig. 2F. When the temperature rises to 70°C, the rapid reduction in PLA’s modulus reduces the IP’s constraint on the RC (see Fig. 2E, middle), thereby transforming the system into a monostable state, as shown by the red curve in Fig. 2F. Ultimately, the RC unfolds, allowing the two particles to separate and complete bond breaking, as depicted by the transition from state (ii) to state (iii) in Fig. 2E.

The FEA of the multiparticle assembly process is challenging due to complex contacts and multiple snap-through events. Consequently, we used an octagonal particle (Fig. 2G, left) to represent the particle depicted in Fig. 1A. In the simulation, cohesive contacts are assigned to the convex (green) and concave (blue) surfaces of the equivalent particle, while the other surfaces are modeled with frictionless hard contacts. When the green and blue surfaces of the two particles touch, this contact establishes a connection, effectively replicating the bond formation of real particles (Fig. 2G, right). Furthermore, the experimentally measured force-displacement curve for tension-induced bond breaking defines the bilinear model for cohesive contacts (Fig. 2H), illustrating the traction-separation law for these two surfaces. Figure 2I demonstrates the bond formation process between two equivalent particles through the FEA. Initially, the upper particle moves toward the lower particle (Fig. 2I, left). This movement facilitates contact between their convex and concave surfaces, leading to bond formation (Fig. 2I, middle). Subsequently, the upper particle moves upward, pulling the lower particle upward to demonstrate the bond stability (Fig. 2I, right).

### Assembly of granular metamaterials by mechanical compression

To assemble the structured particles into granular metamaterials, we first investigated the compression-induced assembly of one-dimensional (1D) granular metamaterials with various configurations (see Fig. 3, A to D, and movie S3) through both experimental tests and FEA. Figure 3A illustrates the assembly of five particles within a straight container through compression, while the corresponding force-displacement response is represented by the black solid line in Fig. 3B. During compression, the five initially loosely packed particles (Fig. 3A, top) are compacted into an interlocked linear configuration (Fig. 3A, middle), with bonds highlighted in red. As shown in Fig. 3B, this process involves several decreases in force, corresponding to the sliding adjustment of particle positions and the snap-throughs induced by compression. Upon load release, a linear granular metamaterial is formed (Fig. 3A, bottom). The assembly process in the straight container under different arrangements is also shown in fig. S19. Expanding beyond straight arrangements, particles were also compressed in S-shaped and U-shaped containers (Fig. 3, C and D; fig. S20; and movie S3). These configurations reveal that the curvature of the container crucially influences the assembled structure, guiding the particles into shapes that mimic the container’s form, thus demonstrating the adaptability and reconfigurability of granular metamaterials.

We further explored the assembly of 2D granular metamaterials (Fig. 3, E to H, and movie S4). Initially, a 2 × 2 array of particles undergoes bidirectional compression using a custom biaxial loading device (Fig. 3E), with the corresponding force-displacement response depicted in Fig. 3F. During compression, the press head prompts the particles to autonomously adjust their positions and results in the locking of the IPs and RCs. The two decreasing steps in force shown in Fig. 3F correspond to the snap-throughs. Upon release, four bonds are formed, connecting the four particles into a unified structure. We also conducted additional experiments to explore more general conditions (see the Supplementary Materials and figs. S21 and S22). In these cases, we varied the initial relative positions of the particles and applied biaxial compression, resulting in a different bonding pattern. This demonstrates the system’s adaptability and robustness toward various initial conditions.

This method can further be expanded to the assembly of a larger number of particles. For instance, the biaxial compression of 25 arbitrarily positioned particles with n = 9 (Fig. 3G) can facilitate bond formation into a holistic structure (see movie S4). For a more general loading method, a zip tie is used to apply circumferential compression for assembly (Fig. 3H and movie S4). By stretching the zip tie, the reduction in its length exerts circumferential compression on the enclosed particles, enabling the bond formation and completing the assembly (Fig. 3H, right). Considering the shape adaptability of discrete particles, this approach also enables the encapsulation of objects (Fig. 3, I and J, and movie S4). As shown in Fig. 3I, a circular object is surrounded by 74 particles, which are then subjected to biaxial compression to encapsulate the target object (see movie S4). Complementing these observations, we performed the FEA of equivalent particles, which provides insights into their encapsulation capabilities and demonstrates the successful encapsulation of both square and triangular objects using various loading methods (Fig. 3J). This adaptability highlights the potential of granular metamaterials for versatile engineering applications where reconfigurability is crucial.

The examples above demonstrate that the assembly process consistently results in stable configurations, although the process is inherently flexible. This flexibility, observed across different container shapes and loading conditions, actually enhances the system’s robustness. It allows the system to achieve reliable and predictable outcomes without requiring precise initial positioning and arrangement.

Last, by modifying the grooves on the particles to be inclined at an angle θ (Fig. 3K), the assembly of granular metamaterials that curve into the third dimension can be achieved. Figure 3K (right) illustrates that two assembled particles can form an inclined bond, with an angle of 160° when θ = 20 ° . Furthermore, granular metamaterials can be assembled into a 3D curved surface (Fig. 3K, bottom). This feature illustrates the feasibility of extending the assemblies into 3D structures, potentially enhancing the structural integrity required in more demanding applications. The observations in Fig. 3 collectively underscore the substantial potential of our granular metamaterials in adaptive and reconfigurable applications, driven by their inherent flexibility and responsiveness to external mechanical stresses.

### Disassembly of granular metamaterials by thermal stimuli

The diverse assembled structures of granular metamaterials demonstrated above maintain their configurations due to the bistability of the RCs within the particles. To enable reconfigurability, these granular metamaterials must have the capability of bond breaking, allowing them to disassemble into discrete particles. Drawing on the heat-induced bond breaking mechanism detailed in Fig. 2, we first explored the disassembly of a 3 × 3 granular metamaterial as an example (Fig. 4A and movie S5). We used a hot air gun to heat the assembled structure from the right side (Fig. 4A, left). As the temperature increased, some bonds between particles started to break, manifesting as outward ejections depicted by the blue-to-red gradient arrows (Fig. 4A, middle). Eventually, all bonds broke, resulting in a transition to a disassembled state (Fig. 4A, right). Next, we explored the sequential ejection of particles by applying localized heating to the granular metamaterial (Fig. 4B and movie S5). Using a fine-tip hot air gun, we performed localized heating sequentially from right to left across the 1D structure, with the heated region indicated in yellow. The particles were observed to eject sequentially along the track of the container. At the moment of ejection, the velocity of the particles was ~0.96 m/s. This process was also visualized using infrared thermography for a more vivid visualization. This process effectively demonstrates a controlled disassembly method via thermal stimuli, where the application of targeted heat results in a precise and orderly separation of particles from the original structure.

Beyond controlling the order of bond breaking through heating locations, we investigated temperature-controlled sequential bond breaking by incorporating additional thermally responsive materials. To this end, we replaced the PLA of the IPs in the particles with polyethylene terephthalate glycol (PETG, Fig. 4C, left), which has a higher Tg of ~80°C (see the Supplementary Materials and fig. S2). To validate this concept, two types of assembled particles, i.e., PLA-based assembly (green) and PETG-based assembly (blue), were placed on a heating platform simultaneously (Fig. 4C, right, and movie S5). In step 1, the platform temperature was maintained at ~70°C, at which the bonds in the PLA-based assembled particles broke while the PETG-based assembly remained intact. In step 2, as the temperature reached 100°C, the more heat-resistant PETG-based bonds began to break, leading to the disassembly of the whole structure. This experiment demonstrates its capability for multistep disassembly. We further constructed an annular structure by combining these two types of particles (Fig. 4D, i). This assembly was subjected to heating on a platform where PLA-based bonds first broke (Fig. 4D, ii), which caused the structure to disassemble into three subassemblies of PETG-based particles (Fig. 4D, iii). Upon further increasing the temperature, these three PETG-based subassemblies disintegrated into discrete individual particles (Fig. 4D, iv). Two-step disassembly of a 5 × 5 granular metamaterial was also demonstrated (fig. S24). This experiment highlights the potential for recycling and reusing materials through disassembly and reassembly, emphasizing the precise control achieved by regulating the heating temperature.

Heat-induced disassembly offers a noncontact and efficient method, especially beneficial for complex systems where mechanical disassembly would be impractical and inefficient. In addition, this approach is scalable and remains its effectiveness even as the system is miniaturized.

### Mechanical performance of the granular metamaterials

Considering the distinct mechanical properties exhibited by granular metamaterials in assembled and unassembled states, it is crucial to quantitatively investigate their mechanical performance under compression, shearing, and bending. We initially focused on the 4 × 4 granular metamaterial under compression and shearing, as depicted in Fig. 5 (A and D). On the basis of the model, we developed specialized loading apparatuses tailored for these experiments (Fig. 5, A and D). The force-displacement relationships during compression are detailed in Fig. 5B, which captures the mechanical behavior in both states. A series of measured shots of the deformed patterns are presented in Fig. 5C, corresponding to load levels (state i to vi) marked on the F-V curve. Under compression, horizontal bonds were prone to breaking due to Poisson’s effect, transitioning from state i to ii (Fig. 5C and movie S6). As compression continues, the structure segregates into four 1 × 4 substructures susceptible to buckling and subsequent bond breaking under further load. In contrast, the unassembled state, formed by simple stacking, lacks inherent interlocks, leading to the peripheral particles collapsing under compression, while some central particles may form bonds (state v to vi in Fig. 5C). In the initial stage of compression, the apparent compression modulus was measured to be ~2.32 MPa for the assembled state and 0.355 MPa for the unassembled state. The force-displacement curves in Fig. 5B demonstrate that the assembled state has substantially higher compressive stiffness than the unassembled state.

The shearing performance is further explored in Fig. 5 (D to F). In the setup, particles on the left are fixed, while those on the right are attached to a loading head, allowing only vertical movement (Fig. 5D and movie S6). In the assembled state, increasing shear strain leads to the breaking of internal bonds (from state i to iii in Fig. 5F). Conversely, in the unassembled state, the particles merely rotate relative to each other under shear (from state iv to vi in Fig. 5F). The measured force-displacement data in Fig. 5E show a notable increase in the apparent shear modulus between the two states. In the initial stage of shearing, the apparent shear modulus was ~0.233 MPa for the assembled state and 0.072 MPa for the unassembled state, indicating that the assembled state has a higher initial resistance to shear deformation.

The bending behaviors of line-shaped and arc-shaped granular metamaterials were also investigated (see Fig. 5, G to I, and fig. S25). The experimental setups, as depicted in Fig. 5G and fig. S25A, were designed to evaluate the bending responses of these materials. During bending tests, the assembled arc-shaped structure experiences sequential bond breaking under increasing compression, while the unassembled, loosely stacked structure collapses instantly due to its lack of integrity (fig. S25C and movie S6). The force-displacement curves shown in fig. S25B demonstrate that the load-bearing capacity of the assembled arc-shaped structure is ~100 times greater than that of the unassembled, stacked structure. In addition, the bending behavior of a line-shaped granular metamaterial composed of 7 × 2 particles was examined, as shown in Fig. 5 (G to I). In this case, the unassembled particles, which cannot form a stable structure through simple stacking, fail to support any load during the bending test. Thus, only the assembled state enables the structure to withstand bending forces and perform successfully in the three-point bending tests. Compared to the arc-shaped structure, the force levels in the line-shaped configuration are much smaller, primarily due to the inherent stability and boundary constraints. The discussion above demonstrates the switchable mechanical properties of granular metamaterials through state transitions, underscoring the potential to engineering advanced materials specifically designed for targeted mechanical and structural applications.

### Collective motion of the granular metamaterials for reconfigurable robots

To enable collective directional movement in granular metamaterials, we introduced an active particle integrated with a drive module, as shown in Fig. 1F. The exploded view (Fig. 6A) illustrates that this active particle is based on a modified bimaterial structured particle. It incorporates an electric motor connected to a wheel for propulsion, a battery for power, and a microcontroller with a signal receiver for acquisition and processing of signals from the remote control. Given that the particle is inclined relative to the ground, applying positive and negative voltages to the motor enables the particle to move in clockwise or counterclockwise rotations (Fig. 6B and movie S7).
