# Robust Bilinear-Noise-Optimal Control for Gravitational-Wave Detectors: A Mixed LQG/ $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ Approach

**Authors:** Ian A. O. MacMillan Email: macmillan@caltech.edu Affiliation: California Institute of Technology, PMA, 1200 E. California Blvd. Pasadena, CA 91125 Lee P. McCuller Affiliation: California Institute of Technology, PMA, 1200 E. California Blvd. Pasadena, CA 91125

## Abstract

At its lowest frequencies, LIGO is limited by noise in its many degrees of freedom of suspended optics, which, in turn, introduce noise in the interferometer through their feedback control systems. Nonlinear interactions are a dominant source of low-frequency noise, mixing noise from multiple degrees of freedom. The lowest-order form is bilinear noise, in which the noise from two feedback-controlled subsystems multiplies to mask gravitational waves. Bilinear couplings require control trade-offs that simultaneously balance high- and low-frequency noise. Currently, there is no known lower limit to bilinear control noise. Here, we develop benchmark cost functions for bilinear noise and associated figures of merit. Linear-quadratic-Gaussian control then establishes aggressive feedback that saturates the lower bounds on the cost functions. We then develop a mixed LQG and $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ approach to directly compute stable, robust, and optimal feedback, using the LIGO’s alignment control system as an example. Direct computations are fast while ensuring a global optimum. By calculating optimal robust control, it is possible to construct the lower bound on controls noise along the Pareto front of practical controllers for LIGO. This method can be used to drastically improve controls noise in existing observatories as well as to set subsystem control noise requirements for next-generation detectors with parameterized design.

#### Keywords:

## I Introduction

The Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory is a ground-based gravitational wave interferometer that first detected gravitational waves in 2015 [1]. Since its first detection, the LIGO Scientific Collaboration has been working to reduce noise in the instrument to increase its sensitivity and, therefore, detect even fainter gravitational wave signals [12, 13]. These significant improvements in Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory’s sensitivity, as well as the inclusion of additional detectors, have led to an increased detection rate that expands astrophysical study [12, 13, 3, 4, 2, 5].

There is considerable interest in reducing low-frequency noise in Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory ( $<$ 30 Hz). There are many low-frequency waveforms, like high-mass binary black hole inspirals, whose detection would benefit from an increased sensitivity in the low-frequency band [22]. Other waveforms that extend to higher frequencies will benefit from higher signal-to-noise detections, improved parameter estimation, and potentially early warning of ongoing events during the low-frequency portion of long-lived waveforms. Currently, at these low frequencies, both Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory detectors are limited by noise introduced by the feedback control loops. Improving the controllers used in Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory’s feedback loops and generally improving the processes for creating these controllers could significantly reduce the low-frequency noise in the detectors as well as allowing for resources to be spent on other areas of improvement.

### I.1 Motivation

The Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory instrumentation community widely uses classical control design methods. While an entire system has many degrees of freedom, they are almost all designed and engineered as individual single-input and single-output signal paths using transfer functions, Bode plots, and frequency-resolved budgets of noise contributions. These subsystems and control loops are designed depending on how they interconnect to affect the principal measurement channels. The software interfaces of Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory are optimized for this approach, and it is largely successful; however, it has several weaknesses. First, the loops are all hand-designed, which can get the system operating fast, but compounds negatively for global optimization. In particular, without a lower bound on performance, a halting criterion for optimizing is established either by experience or by exhaustion. Furthermore, the design of coupled multiple-input and multiple-output systems must often be iterative, as loop shapes and noise consequences are interdependent. More modern state-space controls approaches are an attractive research topic, promising guaranteed existence, stability, and optimality properties even for complicated, inter-coupled multiple-input and multiple-output systems.

So far, modern controls approaches have not been widely adopted due to the unique requirements of gravitational-wave detectors. First, these approaches require very specific cost functions to form well-posed optimization problems. Second, these approaches usually assume white noise inputs; thus, system models must be augmented with noise-shaping filters. The fitting of such filters is nontrivial but now reliable with modern algorithms. The third issue is that interferometers rarely have actuator cost functions (unlike, e.g., aerospace); thus, typical examples of regulator cost do not immediately apply. The fourth issue is that interferometer loops are limited by transmission delays, which create nonminimum-phase zeros that must be incorporated into the control loop design. The final and highly significant hurdle is dynamic range. The range of shaped noise in gravitational-wave detectors spans 8-12 orders of magnitude, from low-frequency seismic motion to interferometric sensors. The combination of these factors causes optimal solutions to sit on the edge of stability regions, where even the best-known numerical algorithms struggle.

### I.2 Approach

This manuscript adopts an intermediate and transitional approach in an effort to supplant hand-tuning while managing these challenges. It uses modern methods to pose and solve a single-input and single-output controls problem. Future work can extend its examples to more intrinsically multiple-input and multiple-output problems. A major focus of this work is the problem definition, to pose the modern controls problem using figures of merit that are relevant to optimize gravitational-wave detectors. Furthermore, the mixed-sensitivity approach we develop is necessary to find robust solvers that have acceptable gain and phase margins. This approach is mathematically complex to describe, but has largely been solved in previous controls literature. By finding solutions with acceptable phase margins, much like our hand-designed controllers, the numerical solutions are generally better behaved and do not live “near the edge” of admissible solution regions, where small perturbations, numerically or in the instrument plants, push them outside. Our mixed-sensitivity solver rapidly arrives at controllers qualitatively similar to hand designs but guaranteed optimal for our defined figures of merit that are tied to the astrophysics objectives.

The organization of this paper is to be a bridge between classical and modern controls approaches. The first half provides the problem setup and results using the language of transfer functions and noise projections. Our results are included in these sections, showing how to form a modern controls optimization problem to minimize bilinear control noise and the resulting sets of controllers. The optimal controllers set bounds on the best possible noise performance, useful for determining a halting point for hand-designs. We then transform the problem description to use a mixed-sensitivity approach, yielding controllers with acceptable and adjustable stability margins. The second half of the paper translates the problem and solutions into state-space form and summarizes the literature and approach required to build our custom mixed-sensitivity numerical solver. This combination of approaches establishes a framework to utilize modern control systems to solve open controls challenges in gravitational-wave detectors.

## II Background

Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory’s sensitivity is limited by the sum of a number of individual noise sources in the interferometer. The extent to which these noise sources obscure astrophysical signals is expressed using the signal-to-noise ratio. The signal-to-noise ratio of a signal can be calculated from the Fourier transform of the event waveform, $h_{\mathrm{gw}}(f)$ , and the power spectral density of the interferometer’s noise, $S_{h}(f)$ , using

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{SNR}^{2} \displaystyle=4\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\left|h_{\mathrm{gw}}(f)\right|^{2}}{S_{h}(f)}df\mathrm{.} $$

The detection range,

$$ \displaystyle d_{\mathrm{range}} \displaystyle=\frac{d_{\mathrm{gw}}}{2.26}\frac{\mathrm{SNR}}{\rho_{0}}\mathrm{,} $$

is the average effective distance to which events louder than a threshold signal-to-noise ratio called $\rho_{0}$ can be detected. The range can be calculated using the signal-to-noise ratio formula and the distance to the fiducial source. For an $h_{\mathrm{gw}}(f)$ waveform modeled from a source at distance $d_{\mathrm{gw}}$ , the detection range averaged over the sky is included above. The threshold signal-to-noise ratio is usually taken to be $\rho_{0}=8$ , and the factor of 2.26 accounts for the average of the interferometer antenna pattern over the sky [17].

The astronomical range is essential to the sensitivity of the interferometer because it dictates the detection rate, $\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{det}}$ , which holds the relations

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{\mathrm{det}}\propto d_{\mathrm{range}}^{3}\propto\mathrm{SNR}^{3}\mathrm{.} $$

Even minor decreases in the interferometer’s noise can have a significant impact on the detection rate. One of Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory’s long-standing goals is increasing the detection rate for binary neutron star inspirals. Binary neutron star waveforms are taken to be the standard fiducial for computing signal-to-noise ratio as a figure of merit for the interferometer performance in this work.

### II.1 Noise from Control Systems

At the low frequency end of its detection band, Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory’s sensitivity is limited by noise injected by control systems. At frequencies below Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory’s detection band, the control systems are stabilizing the operating points of otherwise highly nonlinear optical cavity resonators and interferometers. Noise coming from the control actuation of cavity alignment and auxiliary length are two of the largest of all known noise sources in the detector below 10 Hz [12, 13]. Interferometric controls noise is any noise that arises from the addition of a stabilizing or noise-suppressing controller to a degree of freedom of the interferometer system. When a controller is added in a feedback loop to a degree of freedom, some of the noise inherent to that degree of freedom, along with new measurement noise, passes through the controller and is (re-)injected into the system at the actuator. While a controller can reduce the overall noise of a degree of freedom, it also introduces a new noise source from the controller’s sensor, particularly at higher frequencies corresponding to the feedback bandwidth. For complex systems with many degrees of freedom and many control systems, the controls noise can become a significant noise source. From optics controllers to seismic isolation, each Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory detector has more than 300 controllers that all maintain its operating point but add noise to the principal readout: the differential-arm length. This is the measurement of arm-length differences caused by gravitational waves, and thus the output of interest for astrophysics.

Here, a model is constructed for how a control system for a single degree of freedom affects the signal and introduces noise. We will later express bilinear noise in terms of this model. The plant noise of some degree of freedom under feedback control, $N_{\mathrm{c}}$ , affects the signal seen at the output of the interferometer through

$$ \displaystyle h_{\mathrm{signal}}(f) \displaystyle=h_{\mathrm{gw}}(f)+N_{\mathrm{det}}(f)+C(f)N_{\mathrm{c}}(f)\mathrm{,} $$

where $h_{\mathrm{gw}}(f)$ is a potential signal, $N_{\mathrm{det}}$ is all the detector noise from sources other than the degree of freedom being modeled, and $C(f)$ is a frequency-dependent coupling of the degree of freedom into differential-arm length. This coupling is often indirect and sourced from bilinear effects. For simple estimates, it is often possible to assume $C(f)$ is constant across all frequencies, but in the general case, measurement data necessitates that it be frequency-dependent. An example measurement of $C(f)$ and physical motivation are described in Section III.2. The power spectral density of the total noise in the detector is thus

$$ \displaystyle S_{h}(f) \displaystyle=S_{\mathrm{det}}(f)+|C(f)|^{2}S_{\mathrm{c}}(f)\mathrm{,} $$

where $S_{\mathrm{det}}(f)$ is the power spectral density of all the detector noise from sources other than the degree of freedom being modeled and $S_{\mathrm{c}}(f)$ is the power spectral density of the noise of interest, in this case a definition of controls noise. By linearizing Eq. 1, and including Eq. 5’s expression of $S_{h}(f)$ , the controls noise dependent signal-to-noise ratio becomes

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{SNR}^{2}=\mathrm{SNR}_{\text{det}}^{2}-\mathrm{SNR}^{2}_{\text{lost}}\text{,} $$

where

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{SNR}_{\text{det}}^{2}=4\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\left|h_{\mathrm{gw}}(f)\right|^{2}}{S_{\mathrm{det}}(f)}\ df $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{SNR}_{\text{lost}}^{2}=4\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\left|C\right|^{2}\left|h_{\mathrm{gw}}(f)\right|^{2}}{S_{\mathrm{det}}(f)^{2}}S_{\mathrm{c}}(f)\ df\mathrm{.} $$

Adapting Eq. 2 gives the controls-noise-dependent expression for the detection range lost as

$$ \displaystyle d_{\mathrm{lost}}=\frac{d_{\mathrm{gw}}}{2.26\rho_{0}}\frac{\mathrm{SNR}^{2}_{\text{lost}}}{2\mathrm{SNR}_{\text{det}}}\mathrm{.} $$

The lost detection range can also be computed using the linearization. The point of linearizing the equation is to split it into terms that show the specific impact of a particular noise, $S_{\mathrm{c}}$ , on the signal-to-noise ratio and binary neutron star range. In this equation, $S_{\mathrm{c}}$ can be any noise of interest, assuming it is small enough to keep the linearization accurate. The $S_{\mathrm{c}}$ term is inside an integral that includes a frequency-dependent weighting. That weighting term will later be useful to define a shaping filter for the controls optimization problem in terms of the lost signal-to-noise ratio or range cost.

The root mean squared of a noise from channel $N_{\mathrm{c}}$ , is indicated by $\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{c}}$ . In order to keep the interferometer locked, there is a maximum allowable root mean squared. If the noise in the interferometer exceeds that limit, the interferometer is unable to maintain operation, e.g., sufficient alignment.

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{c}}\equiv\int_{0}^{\infty}S_{\mathrm{c}}(f)df< \displaystyle\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{c,unlock}}\mathrm{.} $$

A fundamental requirement of control systems is to ensure that no binary neutron star exceeds its lock-loss threshold. Thus, there is a tradeoff between operational requirements and noise injection.

There are two primary sources of controls noise: environmental noise and measurement noise. Environmental noise is any noise that acts on the states of the suspended interferometer plant. For example, seismic noise is an environmental noise that is of great concern for ground-based interferometers. Measurement noise is the difference between the measured states of a system and their true value, generally due to an imperfect intermediate sensor used to probe the states. Both the measurement and environmental noise pass through a control filter and then feed back into the system, but measurement noise would not otherwise affect plant states except through the control system actuating it into real plant noise.

Considering only two noise sources is a useful simplification. In reality, there are many noise sources that all contribute differently to every degree of freedom in the interferometer. However, these noise sources can only enter the system in two places: either before the plant (environmental noise) or before the controller (measurement noise). This distinction also aligns with the assumptions and model of a typical optimization using classical control theory to shape the open-loop gain.

Without physically decreasing environmental or measurement noise, which much of the engineering resources Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory is dedicated to, the only way to decrease controls noise is to find an optimal controller, $K$ , such that the minimum amount of noise is fed through into differential-arm length while achieving a total root mean squared goal.

Here we distinguish two channels $N_{\text{p}}$ and $N_{\text{a}}$ . The former, which must meet a noise threshold, is the sum of environmental noise and controller actuation, filtered by the plant’s transfer function. This noise, $N_{\text{p}}$ , is the noise directly seen by the interferometer. The latter, $N_{\text{a}}$ , is the signal sent by an actuator due to its control system, then shaped by the plant’s transfer function, without including direct contributions from environmental noise. These two noises are soon presented visually in Fig. 1. The optimal controller must ensure that the plant’s noise $\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{p}}$ will meet requirements by shaping its spectrum $S_{\mathrm{p}}$ through the environmental and measurement noise contributions.

$$ \displaystyle S_{\mathrm{p}}(f) \displaystyle=\left|\frac{P(f)}{1-G(f)}\right|^{2}S_{\mathrm{env}}(f)+\left|\frac{G(f)}{1-G(f)}\right|^{2}S_{\mathrm{meas}}(f)\text{,} $$

where

$$ \displaystyle G(f) \displaystyle=K(f)P(f) $$

is the open-loop gain of the full system, $P(f)$ is the transfer function of the plant component, either the input or output of $P(f)$ represents the degree of freedom to be controlled, $K(f)$ is the transfer function of the controller, $S_{\mathrm{env}}(f)$ is the power spectral density of the environmental noise, and $S_{\mathrm{meas}}(f)$ is the power spectral density of the measurement noise. Here, it is explicitly indicated that each of these expressions is a function of frequency; this dependence is continued but will not be explicitly stated in the following formulas.

The total plant noise, $N_{\text{p}}$ , which is presented in Eq. 11, is the typical minimization metric for modern controls. It is the measure of all the noise coming out of a system, including all coherent cancellations and interactions. In a system with no cross-coupling to any other degree of freedom, minimizing $S_{\mathrm{p}}$ would minimize the sum of both measurement noise and environment noise injected into the system.

The definition of $N_{\text{p}}$ is often presented as controls noise in modern controls. However, this differs from most previous work in gravitational wave interferometer sensing and control, where controls noise is defined as any noise that passes through the controller and becomes a new contribution through actuation on the degree of freedom. The definition of actuation point controls noise, $S_{\mathrm{a}}$ , is

$$ \displaystyle S_{\mathrm{a}} \displaystyle=\left|\frac{PG}{1-G}\right|^{2}S_{\mathrm{env}}+\left|\frac{G}{1-G}\right|^{2}S_{\mathrm{meas}}\text{,} $$

and

$$ \displaystyle N_{\mathrm{a}} \displaystyle=\frac{PG}{1-G}N_{\mathrm{env}}+\frac{G}{1-G}N_{\mathrm{meas}}\text{.} $$

The actuation point controls noise definition is useful because optimizing to reduce it is more directly a means of penalizing actuation, as $K$ is in the numerator of both environmental and measurement noise contributions to Eqs. 13 and 14. In large multi-degree of freedom coupled systems like Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory, it is often true that actuation on one degree of freedom can inject noise into another. The power spectral density $S_{\mathrm{c}}$ , from Eq. 6, could be set equal to any noise of interest like $S_{\mathrm{p}}$ ; however in this paper $S_{\mathrm{c}}=S_{\mathrm{a}}$ as is appropriate for the alignment-control degree of freedom we investigate and as typical for gravitational wave controls. The noise from this metric, $N_{\mathrm{a}}$ , is then used as the noise, $N_{\mathrm{a}}$ , in Eq. 4. An approach more widely used in modern controls that only uses $S_{\mathrm{p}}$ as an optimization metric is discussed in Appendix B.

In this work, both $S_{\mathrm{a}}$ and $S_{\mathrm{p}}$ will be used. The former for the control effect on SNR and BNS range, and the latter for the minimization of the total root mean squared, $\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{p}}$ from Eq. 10, needed to maintain the operating point. Finding a “best” controller is difficult because of the trade-off between suppressing environmental noise in $S_{\mathrm{p}}$ with a large $K$ and suppressing measurement noise in $S_{\mathrm{a}}$ with a small $K$ . Finding the optimal controller requires a multi-objective optimization: the root mean squared controls noise, $\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{p}}$ , and the binary neutron star detection range.

### II.2 Application to Alignment Sensing Control System

Controls noise associated with the alignment sensing control system is one of the largest sources of controls noise at low frequencies [12, 13]. The alignment sensing control system is responsible for keeping the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory test masses aligned in their angular degrees of freedom. Each Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory interferometer has eight principal control filters dedicated to maintaining angular stability in the arm cavities. These eight control filters are the product of three distinguishing degrees. Each system is either in pitch or yaw (P/Y) rigid-body rotation, Differential or Common motion between the two Michelson arms (C/D), and either HARD or SOFT spring reaction to motion.

HARD modes are when the two test masses that make up Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory’s Fabry-Pérot arm cavities rotate in opposite directions, e.g., one rotates very slightly up, and the other rotates very slightly down. Since Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory’s Fabry-Pérot cavities have a high g-factor, the differential rotation causes a rotation of the optical axis, and radiation pressure pushes the arms back towards their nominal angle. Thus, HARD modes increase suspension stiffness and occur at higher frequencies. SOFT modes are the opposite, where the mirrors move at a common angle, which translates the cavity axis. The translation moves the beam off center and produces a negative spring constant (anti-spring).

The name of each mode is the composition of these distinguishing degrees. I.e., CSOFTY is the common soft mode in the yaw angular tilt. In this study, only the DHARD yaw controller is calculated. The choice of actuation point noise optimization for the DHARD yaw degree of freedom presented in this paper was motivated by the strong coupling between angular actuation and length in Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory Hanford’s arms.

## III Problem Formulation

The heart of the controls noise problem is straightforward to outline: too much measurement noise gets passed through the controller and is actuated spuriously into the differential-arm length degree of freedom, injecting noise. As with all Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory systems, the goal is to minimize the noise that is fed into the readouts of the interferometer that contain information of astrophysical importance, mainly the differential-arm length readout. The solution to this control problem is more difficult, as it must account for many different factors, including the plant’s response, the measurement noise passed through the control system, and the system’s stability and robustness.

The modern controls optimization method that is well-suited to this problem is linear quadratic Gaussian control. An linear quadratic Gaussian controller is the optimal linear controller for a system that is disturbed by Gaussian white noise and has a quadratic (root mean squared-like) cost function. Described in Sections VI.2 and VI.3, linear quadratic Gaussian controllers minimize a system’s $\mathcal{H}_{2}$ norm, which is a measure of the root mean squared at system outputs from all of its noise inputs. The “ $\mathcal{H}$ ” stands for solutions within a Hardy space, indicating that the system must be closed-loop stable. This is necessary to have well-posed noise in the time domain, and appropriate for implementable feedback controllers. The typical quadratic cost function for LQG is based on the total noise root mean squared, $S_{\text{p}}$ , of a degree of freedom. Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory’s performance relies on multiple criteria, so we will use a weighted root mean squared that includes both the total noise and the lost detection range as figures of merit.

So far, the noise model of Section II.1 has not included the nonlinear/bilinear aspects. It has simply been a model of direct, linear noise coupling, which should naively only be optimized for the binary neutron star range while ignoring the degree of freedom root mean squared. The following sections investigate how to incorporate a weighted root mean squared to balance noise suppression against control noise injection.

When creating a single-input and single-output controller for a single degree of freedom, a multiple-input and multiple-output system is constructed that takes into account the multiple inputs that can affect the degree of freedom, as well as multiple outputs to measure its performance. This system, whose block diagram is presented in Fig. 1, includes all of the information that is used to find the optimal controller, mainly of three types: the noise in the system, the plant of the system, and the figures of merit of the system. The full system model, outlined by the dashed grey box in Fig. 1, includes four inputs, a control input, $u_{c}$ , a measurement noise input, $u_{n1}$ , a state noise input (environmental noise), $u_{n2}$ , and an $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ disturbance input. Both noise inputs are white noise inputs that pass through shaping filters to model the measurement and environmental noise. The control input, $u_{\mathrm{c}}$ is connected to the output of the controller and is not a white noise input. The $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ disturbance input, $u_{\infty}$ , serves as a port for the solver to inject unshaped signals into the system and is a necessity for optimal control analyzed later. The system has two types of outputs: the figure of merit outputs and the measured output, $y_{\text{meas}}$ . $y_{\text{meas}}$ gives the state of the plant with added measurement noise. Measurement noise is only observed by the controller and represents an imperfect estimate of the plant’s true state.

The system layout includes multiple blocks, each representing a transfer function. The plant, $P$ , represents the physical system being simulated; in this case, it is the mechanism by which the actuator converts force/torque inputs into displacements/tilts. The measurement noise, $M$ , is the shaping filter that turns the input Gaussian white noise into the appropriately shaped sensing noise, while the environmental noise, $E$ , serves the same purpose for the state noise on the plant, both shown in Fig. 2. The transfer functions relate to Eqs. 11, 13, and 14 through

$$ \displaystyle S_{\mathrm{env}} \displaystyle=\left|E\right|^{2}S^{u}_{n1} $$

and

$$ \displaystyle S_{\mathrm{meas}} \displaystyle=\left|M\right|^{2}S^{u}_{n2}\mathrm{,} $$

where

$$ \displaystyle S^{u}_{n1}\text{, }S^{u}_{n2} \displaystyle\equiv 1/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}} $$

and are uncorrelated. This indicates that these inputs are driven by Gaussian white noise that is then shaped by the relevant noise-shaping filters. The two figure of merit filters, $F_{\mathrm{BNS}}$ and $F_{\mathrm{flat}}$ , represent the transfer function that weights the frequency domain signal properly for two different measures of the controller’s performance described in Section III.2.

The two figure of merit outputs are free of any direct measurement noise, and they are each connected to a point representing the $N_{\text{p}}$ , and $N_{\text{a}}$ plant and actuator noise terms of Eqs. 13, 14, and 11. The frequency response of the plant must have two copies in our model to produce the different contributions of $K$ (to be designed) in the expressions of $N_{\mathrm{a}}$ and $N_{\mathrm{p}}$ .

The Figure of Merit block includes a shaping filters for each path that weight the relative contribution of $S_{a}$ or $S_{p}$ in the optimization problem. The construction and weighting of the figure of merit filters is described in Section III.2 and is fundamental to finding the Pareto front of optimal controllers for a given system. The absence of measurement noise indicates that the figure of merit outputs report the true value (up to weighting) of the degree of freedom from which it is constructed and not what would be observed through an imperfect physical measurement.

For this alignment control application, the state of the plant at $N_{\mathrm{p}}$ represents the total angular motion of the mirror or cavity in its degree of freedom (Differential, HARD, Yaw). A flat filter representing the first figure of merit then has $y_{{}_{\mathrm{FOM1}}}$ , which integrates into the total variance of the mirror motion. This is the typical objective that is minimized in LQG/ $\mathcal{H}2$ optimal control. The $N_{\mathrm{a}}$ connection to $y_{{}_{\mathrm{FOM2}}}$ represents how the control actuation pushes on the mirror in pitch or yaw. If the beam is miscentered, the alignment actuation is converted into length noise. The BNS FOM then contains a weighing filter for how important this length noise conversion is for the SNR or range figure of merit.

### III.2 Figures of Merit

As discussed in the previous sections, figures of merit are measures of the performance of a closed-loop system. In the example presented in this paper, an essential new complexity is added: multiple figures of merit.

In the model of the system, shown in Fig. 1, two figures of merit are shown, which have been indicated by Eqs. 6 and 10. Shown inside the red dashed outline in Fig. 1 and represented by transfer functions, these two figures of merit, $F_{\mathrm{BNS}}$ and $F_{\mathrm{flat}}$ , allow for different frequency weightings of the output signal. Fig. 3 shows the magnitude of the two figures of merit used in the augmented alignment sensing control system. The first broadband figure of merit, $F_{\mathrm{flat}}$ , is required to minimize $\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{p}}$ which is necessary to preserve the inequality in Eq. 10. The broadband figure of merit represents the unshaped total noise in the degree of freedom seen after the plant, which affects the operational locking of the interferometer. This figure of merit is also necessary in order for the problem to be well-posed for optimal control, ensuring Assumption 4 in Section VI.3.

The second figure of merit, passing through $F_{\text{BNS}}$ , is a measure of how much the alignment actuation influences the signal-to-noise ratio or range of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory detector to an inspiral of two $1.4~M_{\odot}$ neutron stars at a distance of 40 Mpc, using Eqs. 6-8. The inspiral determines the function $h_{\text{gw}(f)}$ . The factor $C(f)$ is a coupling factor for actuation point control noise into DARM, computed using noise budget data from [13]. $S_{\mathrm{det}}$ is the detector’s noise power spectral density. We fit the weighting filter so that

$$ \displaystyle\left|F_{\text{BNS}}(f)\right|=2\frac{\left|C(f)\right|\left|h_{\mathrm{gw}}(f)\right|}{S_{\mathrm{det}}(f)}\cdot\frac{d_{\mathrm{gw}}}{16\cdot 2.26\cdot\mathrm{SNR}_{\text{det}}}\text{,} $$

where the first term creates a weight filter to compute the $\text{SNR}_{\text{lost}}$ , and the second term converts to lost range.

By connecting to the $N_{\mathrm{a}}$ actuation-point noise, the total variance of $y_{{}_{\mathrm{FOM2}}}$ then produces the lost SNR or lost range. Practically, this filter (seen in Fig. 3) has a dynamic range going from low to high frequencies that spans more than the 16 orders of magnitude of a double-precision float, creating issues that we detail in the following sections.

The frequency-dependent coupling function $C(f)$ is measured through an excitation injected into the control loop [13]. When excited, $S_{\mathrm{a}}$ from Eq. 13 becomes

$$ \displaystyle S_{\mathrm{a}\text{, exc}} \displaystyle=S_{\mathrm{a}}+\left|\frac{G}{1-G}\right|^{2}S_{\mathrm{exc}}\mathrm{,} $$

where $S_{\mathrm{exc}}$ is the power spectral density of the excited signal summed in before the controller. When this excitement is added, $S_{h}$ from Eq. 5 becomes

$$ \displaystyle S_{h\text{, exc}} \displaystyle=S_{\mathrm{det}}+|C|^{2}\left(S_{\mathrm{a}}+\left|\frac{G}{1-G}\right|^{2}S_{\mathrm{exc}}\right)\mathrm{.} $$

From Eqs. 19 and 20, $|C|^{2}$ can be calculated and fit from

$$ \displaystyle|C|^{2}=\frac{S_{h\text{, exc}}-S_{h}}{S_{\mathrm{a}\text{, exc}}-S_{\mathrm{a}}}\mathrm{.} $$

#### III.2.1 Pareto Front of Multiple FOMs for Bilinear Noise

To fully motivate the use of these two figures of merit in the bilinear noise case, Eq. 6 can be rewritten to directly depend on both figures of merit. Consider the noise coupling factor $C$ from Eq. 8. For the multiplication effect that occurs for bilinear noise on a single degree of freedom, a model is assumed where $C\propto\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{p}}$ represents an intermodulation effect. The effect of an intermodulation can be seen by rewriting Eq. 4 in the time domain, with the control noise term becoming bilinear

$$ \displaystyle h_{\mathrm{signal}}(t) \displaystyle=h_{\mathrm{gw}}(t)+N_{\mathrm{det}}(t)+\chi N_{\mathrm{a}}(t)N_{\mathrm{p}}(t)\mathrm{.} $$

Where $\chi$ is a scale factor for the cross-coupling. For our alignment example, $N_{\mathrm{p}}$ is the residual angular motion of the mirror, while $N_{\mathrm{a}}$ is the actuated tilt. If the residual angular motion is non-zero, then the applied tilt causes a coupling to arm length.

When the $N_{\mathrm{p}}$ noise is dominated by low-frequency components, this term becomes $\chi\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{p}}N_{\mathrm{a}}(t)$ by linearizing. See Appendix A for a formal derivation. This substitution can then be used in Eq. 8 via $C(f)=\chi(f)\cdot\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{p}}$ . In the alignment control example problem, this relation for constructing $C(f)$ yields the coupling factor called “A2L” for alignment-to-length. This factor is measured [13] and translates angular motion in the alignment system into length motion in the differential-arm length gravitational wave channel. This form for $C$ and similar models of root mean squared-dependent coupling factors indicates that one aspect of the range depends on the root mean squared as computed from the flat figure of merit, while the other depends on the root mean squared as computed from the shaped binary neutron star figure of merit.

Assuming this form of the $C$ coupling function, the signal-to-noise ratio loss of Eq. 8 becomes

$$ \displaystyle\mathrm{SNR}_{\mathrm{lost}}^{2} \displaystyle=4\cdot\tilde{R}^{2}_{\mathrm{p}}\cdot\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\left|\chi\right|^{2}\left|h_{\mathrm{gw}}(f)\right|^{2}}{S^{2}_{\mathrm{det}}(f)}S_{\mathrm{c}}(f)\ \mathrm{d}\!f \displaystyle=\underbrace{\int_{0}^{\infty}\left|F_{\mathrm{flat}}\right|^{2}S_{\mathrm{p}}\ df}_{\tilde{R}^{2}_{\mathrm{flat}}}\cdot\underbrace{\int_{0}^{\infty}\left|F_{\mathrm{BNS}}\right|^{2}S_{\mathrm{c}}\ \mathrm{d}\!f}_{\tilde{R}^{2}_{\mathrm{BNS}}/\overline{R}^{2}_{\mathrm{flat}}}\mathrm{,} $$

where $\tilde{R}^{2}_{\mathrm{flat}}$ is the RMS of the total plant motion during control and $\overline{R}^{2}_{\mathrm{flat}}$ is a constant for RMS at the time of the measurement of the A2L coupling factor $C(f)$ .

As a minimization problem, a necessary condition for optimality can be established by taking the derivative with respect to the controller parameters $\mathbf{K}$ , in bold to represent parameters in a state-space matrix form. Setting these derivatives to zero finds an extremal point of the noise as

$$ \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=\frac{1}{4|\chi|^{2}}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{K}}\mathrm{SNR}_{\mathrm{lost}}^{2} \displaystyle=\tilde{R}^{2}_{\mathrm{flat}}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{K}}\tilde{R}^{2}_{\mathrm{BNS}}+\tilde{R}^{2}_{\mathrm{BNS}}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{K}}\tilde{R}^{2}_{\mathrm{flat}}\mathrm{.} $$

This relation can be satisfied through the equivalence

$$ \displaystyle 0=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{K}}\tilde{R}^{2}_{\mathrm{syn}}\text{,} $$

when

$$ \displaystyle\zeta \displaystyle\equiv\frac{\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{BNS}}}{\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{flat}}}\mathrm{.} $$

The linear quadratic Gaussian and mixed-sensitivity approaches below find control systems that meet this necessary condition. By scanning over the weight parameter $\zeta$ , the Pareto front of optimal controllers is produced. The above derivation indicates that the bilinear-optimal controller exists along this Pareto front.

There are multiple reasons why the parameter $\zeta$ should be abstracted as an independent term for Eq. 29. The main reason is that, prior to optimization, the ratio of the root mean squared values of the two figures of merit cannot be known. Thus, there is no presumptive $\zeta$ to target. Since linear quadratic Gaussian can only optimize over a single parameter, all of a system’s figures of merit must be combined. With $\zeta$ , we can define a synthetic weighted root mean squared of the two figures of merit, which meaningfully relates to the above condition on the derivative of the signal-to-noise ratio.

$$ \displaystyle\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{syn}}^{2}=\zeta^{2}\tilde{R}_{F_{\mathrm{BNS}}}^{2}+\tilde{R}_{F_{\mathrm{flat}}}^{2}\mathrm{,} $$

The weighted sum of the two figure of merit outputs creates a single synthetic output with its own root mean squared, $\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{syn}}$ . The problem now boils down to a problem to minimize $\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{syn}}$ over many given weightings of $\zeta$ . It is advantageous to only weight one of the figures of merit to achieve the desired relative weighting because leaving the weighting of the flat figure of merit untouched allows for consistent $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ norms across different weightings, which will be important in Section V.1.

For values of $\zeta$ that are zero, or very large, the optimization of $\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{syn}}$ will find the minimum root mean squared in one of the respective figures of merit. Because the root mean squared values satisfy a minimization constraint, the optimized values of both $\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{BNS}}$ and $\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{flat}}$ are expected to be monotonic but not necessarily smooth or convex in $\zeta$ .

Together, this suggests that scanning $\zeta$ will allow one to find the global minimum of the lost signal-to-noise ratio, but doesn’t establish that the control-optimal signal-to-noise ratio loss function is a convex optimization problem in $\zeta$ . For any more complex dependence of $C$ on $\chi$ or $\tilde{R}_{c}$ , the derivative argument above is expected to still apply, but the relationship of Eq. 27 will become more complex. Finally, the above derivation and example based on the $C$ coupling parameter assume only a single degree of freedom. More elaborate models of the $C$ parameter are likely dependent on the root mean squared of multiple degrees of freedom. Thus, the decision point of where to balance flat root mean squared vs. the binary neutron star-weighted root mean squared is, in general, more complex. These are major reasons that $\zeta$ should be treated abstractly to produce a Pareto front. The following plots show that the $\zeta$ parametrization clearly shows the boundary of the optimal space for the two major root mean squared contributions. Thus, scanning $\zeta$ to find a boundary that shows the specific tradeoff between flat-weighted root mean squared and the binary neutron star-weighed root mean squared is the most generally useful expression and is achieved through the $\zeta$ parameter. We believe the above argument can apply to multiple-input and multiple-output systems using a vector of $\zeta$ scales, but leave this for future work.

## IV LQG Optimization

The linear quadratic Gaussian problem is to find an optimal controller that yields the lowest $\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{syn}}$ for a given $\zeta$ . This is equivalent to finding a controller that minimizes the $\mathcal{H}_{2}$ norm of a transfer-function-matrix, $\mathbf{T}_{2}(f)$ , from the $u_{n1},u_{n2}$ vector of inputs, to the $y_{{}_{\mathrm{FOM1}}},y_{{}_{\mathrm{FOM2}}}$ vector of outputs, with a $\zeta$ scaling first applied to the $y_{{}_{\mathrm{FOM2}}}$ output.

By contrast, linear quadratic Gaussian is often taught and presented starting from the separation principle, combining a Kalman filter as a noise-optimal state linear-quadratic estimator with a linear quadratic regulator that minimizes an actuator cost function. The actuator cost is often described as fuel consumption, but when using the figure of merit weighting filters, it can also be interpreted as part of a noise-minimization procedure. This interpretation of linear quadratic Gaussian as an $\mathcal{H}_{2}$ noise minimization procedure can be established intrinsically through minimization [7], as well as through the case analysis of the separation principle [15].

The $\mathcal{H}_{2}$ optimization can prove difficult by hand or even with a gradient-descent numerical optimizer because of design trade-offs. Finding the perfect balance between suppressing environmental noise and introducing minimal measurement noise, all while weighting the output by two figures of merit, is a job that optimal control can perform in a single algebraic solution step. Here,linear quadratic Gaussian is used to find the optimal controller to give the lowest possible $\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{syn}}$ . The control transfer function, $K$ , is determined by the state-space description of the control, $\mathbf{K}_{\mathrm{LQG}}$ , using the method described in Section VI.3. The method of the numerical solver is not essential to understanding the results of this paper, but an important point is that linear quadratic Gaussian optimization is non-iterative. This is essential for speed, as our method requires a scan over the $\zeta$ parameter that indicates the tradeoff between two figures of merit. Because of dynamic range and numerical challenges, an understanding of the numerical solver has been essential to implement this work with a reliable software implementation, but ideally, it should not be required for end users.

### IV.2 Properties and Limitations Apparent in LQG Controllers

All of the calculated controllers aim to reduce the noise of the current hand-tuned Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory DHARD yaw controller. Figs. 4-6 show the root mean squared, open, and closed-loop transfer functions for the linear quadratic Gaussian controllers and for the hand-tuned Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory controller. The properties exhibited by the linear quadratic Gaussian controllers should be related to the hand-tuned controller, but might also inform future design.

The pieces of information that motivate the hand-tuning of the controllers are generally the root mean squared of $S_{p}$ , the open, and closed-loop transfer function to see the stability margins, as well as the noise spectrum presented in Fig. 2. The hand-tuned controller has an integrator under 1 Hz to suppress the most significant contribution to the total root mean squared: tilt noise. The unity-gain frequency of the open-loop gain is below 10 Hz, and the hand-tuned controller rolls off rapidly above 10 Hz to decrease the impact on the observing range. The roll-off enforces a hand-tuned version of the $F_{\mathrm{BNS}}$ weighting, $\zeta$ , but costs a lot of phase at the unity-gain frequency. The hand-tuned controllers sometimes are designed with multiple unity-gain frequency crossings to target noise peaks where needed, but these are challenging to keep stable, so hand design often just suppresses the lowest-frequency noise.

The linear quadratic Gaussian controllers have a much more aggressive open-loop gain. There is a strong roll-off after 10 Hz to minimize the impact on the binary neutron star range, meaning the rate of the roll-off is highly dependent on $\zeta$ . When $\zeta$ is very low and thus the $F_{\mathrm{BNS}}$ does not contribute much to the total root mean squared of $\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{syn}}$ , the roll-off is almost nonexistent. The limit on when the roll-off becomes non-negligible is when $\zeta\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{BNS}}$ becomes larger than the residual environmental noise $\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{p}}$ . One of the most noticeable characteristics of the linear quadratic Gaussian controllers is that they are aggressive. The closed-loop gain, shown in Fig. 6, shows that the unchecked gain peaking can get to about 70 times its DC gain, which corresponds to an unacceptable phase margin of around a few degrees.

## V Solution With Custom Stability Margins

While the goal of many of Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory’s control loops is to minimize the $\mathcal{H}_{2}$ norm of the closed-loop system, optimally, for bilinear noise, the controllers must also be robust and stable. When hand-designing control loops, the measures of this robustness are the gain and phase margins. The gain margin is the smallest gain shift that makes the system unstable, and the phase margin is the smallest amount of phase lag that causes the system to become unstable.

The pure linear quadratic Gaussian solutions for the system, presented in Section IV.1, show unacceptable stability margins and gain peaking. The best controller for many of Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory’s applications would be an linear quadratic Gaussian controller if there were a way to guarantee its stability margins. Unfortunately, to quote the entire abstract of J. Doyle’s paper on guaranteed margins for linear quadratic Gaussian controllers, “There are none” [14].

We must instead employ a more complicated strategy. The phase margin for the system is directly linked to the peak of the closed-loop gain. This peak can be measured using an $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ norm and can be bounded. The following work mixes such a bound within the linear quadratic Gaussian solution and presents robust and noise-optimal controllers for our example alignment (alignment sensing control) system, and can be used for many other Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory’s other control systems.

### V.1 $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ Optimization Problems

Before describing the mixed-sensitivity approach, it is worth first describing the pure $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ optimization approach and contrast it to the $\mathcal{H}_{2}$ minimization performed by linear quadratic Gaussian. In changing an linear quadratic Gaussian problem to utilize an $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ -optimal solver, the same transfer function $\mathbf{T}_{2}(f)$ of noise inputs to figure of merit outputs can be used. The optimization objective is then to find the controller that minimizes the maximum value of $\|\mathbf{T}_{2}(f)\|_{2}$ over all frequencies $f$ (cf. Section VI.6). $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ optimization is typically claimed to find controllers more robust to model changes or adversarial inputs; however, it requires its own precise and uniquely defined figures of merit to be applicable or relatable to astrophysics metrics of gravitational-wave detectors. In particular, $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ makes no guarantees about minimizing root mean squared noise levels and is thus fundamentally unrelated to SNR and detection range metrics.

In effect, when using noise shaping filters and figure of merit weights, a simple reinterpretation of an $\mathcal{H}_{2}$ model into $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ neither improves robustness nor helps with the true noise optimization problem. One must instead use a different set of weights and shapes to define a $\mathbf{T}_{\infty}$ transfer function matrix that is dedicated to the $H_{\infty}$ optimization. The following sections show the mixed-sensitivity approach that retains the $\mathbf{T}_{2}(f)$ of the $\mathcal{H}_{2}$ optimization while including a dedicated weighting to apply an $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ bound. In the following, $\mathbf{T}_{\infty}$ is implemented by utilizing the additional input: $u_{\infty}$ of Fig. 1.

What, then, is the difference between an $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ optimization and a bound? Both applications of $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ use an additional single parameter, $\gamma$ , to apply the bounded real lemma [47] and produce algebraic Riccati equations that only have an admissible solution when $|\mathbf{T}_{\infty}(f)|^{2}_{2}<\gamma^{2}$ for all $f$ . The $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ optimization problem is to find the smallest $\gamma$ , and associated controller, such that these equations hold. In finding the minimal admissible $\gamma$ , there is no remaining freedom in the controller to also optimize an linear quadratic Gaussian $\mathcal{H}_{2}$ problem and minimize noise root mean squared due to the uniqueness of the optimal $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ controller. When a $\gamma$ above the minimum value is chosen, there is a large class of $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ -sub-optimal controllers [19], all related through a $\gamma$ -bounded linear fraction transformations [47], that can be considered as the admissible set for an $\mathcal{H}_{2}$ noise optimization problem. In this way, it is possible to find a solution with a minimal $\mathcal{H}_{2}$ norm within the set of $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ -sub-optimal controllers.

### V.2 LQG Optimal Solutions Given an $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ Performance Bound

As discussed in Section V.1, placing a limit on a suitably defined $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ norm can enforce stability margins of a system. However, $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ solvers do not return controllers with acceptable noise. The ideal controller for most of Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory’s control loops would be the optimal linear quadratic Gaussian filter that has an $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ norm enforcing robustness. Here, a bound on the phase margin is derived, and results from the alignment control model are shown. Section VII describes the numerical method for calculating the optimal solution [10, 21].

The phase margin, $\phi_{m}$ , of the system is expressed as the phase when the magnitude crosses the unity-gain frequency, or expressed as an equation,

$$ \displaystyle\phi_{m}=\angle G(f_{\mathrm{u}})\mathrm{,} $$

where $f_{\mathrm{u}}$ is the unity-gain frequency. As the unity-gain frequency is approached

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{f\rightarrow f_{\mathrm{u}}}|G(f)|=1\mathrm{,} $$

meaning, at $f_{\mathrm{u}}$ , the closed-loop gain is at or near its maximum. If a bound is added to the closed-loop gain and the phase margin is considered in radians, then

$$ \displaystyle\left|\frac{G(f)}{1-G(f)}\right|\leq\gamma $$

and

$$ \displaystyle\lim_{f\rightarrow f_{\mathrm{u}}}\left|\frac{G(f)}{1-G(f)}\right|\approx\frac{1}{|\phi_{m}|}\text{,} $$

yeilding

$$ \displaystyle|\phi_{m}| \displaystyle\geq\frac{1}{\gamma}\text{.} $$

By limiting how large $\gamma$ can be through the controller, the phase margin is also limited. For example, $\gamma\approx 1.27$ limit enforces a $\pi/4=45$ degree phase margin.

To implement this, the additional $u_{\infty}$ input of Fig. 1 is employed. By using the transfer function matrix from the input $u_{\infty}$ to the $y_{{}_{\mathrm{FOM1}}}$ output to define $\mathbf{T}_{\infty}(f)$ , the ideal $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ -bound can be established in the definitions above.

The results, presented in Figs. 7, 8, and 9, show a number of controllers of varying $\zeta$ and $\gamma$ values. Shifting these two parameters allows a group of controllers to be calculated. A single preferred controller can then be post-selected from the group to meet the desired outcome. These plots look similar to those in Section IV, but include a varying $\gamma$ bound as a parameter.

Interestingly, our configuration of $\mathbf{T}_{\infty}(f)$ to measure the closed-loop gain allows even $\gamma=0$ to be admissible, which occurs when $G=0$ , everywhere. In practice, no interesting control loops that influence or optimize the root mean squared can be created as $\gamma\rightarrow 1$ . Numerically, our solver becomes increasingly fragile in this limit. Our procedure is to first choose a moderately large $\gamma$ value, and then solve for a controller. If this solve is successful, then it chooses a smaller value and tries again. $\gamma$ is successively reduced towards $\gamma=1$ until it cannot reliably converge to a solution. For this alignment sensing control example, phase margins of around $45$ degrees are achieved.

### V.3 Properties and Limitations of $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ Norm Limited LQG Controllers

The first and most important change from the pure linear quadratic Gaussian controllers to the controllers presented in Fig. 7, is the improved phase margin. At the lowest $\gamma$ values, the phase margin can beat the margins of the current hand-tuned controller.

As seen in the closed-loop transfer function, the $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ norm is being suppressed as the $\gamma$ value decreases, enforcing an upper limit. The limiting of the $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ norm is not seen in the plot of the closed-loop gain of the pure linear quadratic Gaussian controllers in Fig. 6, since there is no $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ boundary enforced. The enforcement of the limit directly leads to more robust controllers as measured by the gain margin and phase margin.

While the linear quadratic Gaussian results in Section IV.1 show controllers that do not show all of the same features of the current hand-tuned Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory controller, the $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ bounded controllers show many of the same features. In the open-loop transfer function (Fig. 8), the roll-off of the hand-tuned and $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ bounded controllers is very similar in frequency and magnitude. This similarity appears even though $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ bounded controllers’ root mean squared is calculated from $N_{\mathrm{a}}$ rather than $u_{\mathrm{c}}$ , as is often used in Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory’s controller optimization. This similarity may suggest that this distinction is not as important. At very low frequencies, the $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ bounded controllers are actually slightly less aggressive than the hand-tuned controller. As $\gamma$ decreases, the $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ bounded controllers get less aggressive.

A notable difference between the current hand-tuned Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory controller and the calculated $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ bounded controllers is their behavior around unity gain ( $G=1$ ). The hand-tuned controller causes many unity-gain crossings in the open-loop gain as the gain peaks over the line to target noise peaks. Only the $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ bounded controllers with the lowest $\gamma$ values exhibit this behavior.

It is important to note that the solver employed does not exactly implement the gain-peaking constraints that enforce phase margin. Our implementation is slightly more restrictive. Current numerical solution methods for the mixed-sensitivity problem cannot fully independently define $\mathbf{T}_{2}$ and $\mathbf{T}_{\infty}$ . Therefore, our method also has to include the $y_{{}_{\mathrm{FOM2}}}$ output, which instead implements the constraint

$$ \displaystyle\left|\frac{G(f)}{1-G(f)}\right|^{2} \displaystyle\leq\frac{\gamma^{2}}{|F_{\mathrm{flat}}(f)|^{2}+\zeta^{2}|F_{\mathrm{BNS}}(f)|^{2}}\mathrm{.} $$

This could be corrected using a compensating weighting filter on the $u_{\infty}$ input, but this increases the number of system states, requires more computation, and requires a more advanced set of numerical equations. The existing results are satisfactory, though slightly more constrained than necessary to enforce a stability requirement.

## VI Riccati Equation Approach to Mixed-Sensitivity Controls

This paper, so far, presents results and explores the linear quadratic Gaussian, $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ , and mixed linear quadratic Gaussian/ $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ controls problem from the view of classical controls. To numerically solve these problems, the tools and methods of modern controls must be employed. This section explains how the above results were obtained in a way that is useful to a reader trying to replicate or further develop the techniques. This section is not essential to understand the results given above. Notably, additional transformations on the system in Fig. 1 are required to meet the structure and conditions of an linear quadratic Gaussian problem.

We start with the definitions and rules for establishing a well-posed linear quadratic Gaussian problem, relating them to the physical requirements and necessary arrangements on the state diagrams. Additional considerations are required to enforce and solve the $\mathcal{H}_{\infty}$ bounds. The system is then extended to the mixed-sensitivity problem.

### VI.1 State-Space System Description

To define an linear quadratic Gaussian problem, the “System Model” component of Fig. 1 must be assembled into a monolithic state-space. All of the component subsystems are individually modeled or fit from data and converted to state-space form. They are then connected according to the diagram using composition rules, and the entire system, excluding the controller, is put into the form:

$$ \displaystyle\dot{\vec{x}} \displaystyle=\mathbf{A}\vec{x}+{\mathbf{B}_{1}}{\vec{u}}_{i}+{\mathbf{B}_{2}}{\vec{u}}_{\mathrm{c}} \displaystyle{\vec{y}}_{{}_{\mathrm{FOM}}} \displaystyle={\mathbf{C}_{1}}\vec{x}+{\mathbf{D}_{12}}\vec{u}_{\mathrm{c}} \displaystyle{\vec{y}}_{\mathrm{meas}} \displaystyle=\mathbf{C}_{2}\vec{x}+\mathbf{D}_{21}{\vec{u}}_{i}+{\mathbf{D}_{22}}\vec{u}_{\mathrm{c}} $$

where $\mathbf{A}$ is the $n\times n$ state matrix, $\mathbf{B}_{j}$ is the $n\times m_{j}$ input matrix, $\mathbf{C}_{i}$ is the $p_{i}\times n$ sensing matrix, $\mathbf{D}_{ij}$ is the $p_{i}\times m_{j}$ feed-through matrix, $\vec{x}$ is the state vector, ${\vec{u}}_{\mathrm{c}}$ is the control input, ${\vec{u}}_{i}$ is the vector of inputs for simulating noise in your system, ${\vec{y}}_{{}_{\mathrm{FOM}}}$ is the vector of figure of merit outputs, and ${\vec{y}}_{\mathrm{meas}}$ is the measured output. Using $s=2\pi jf$ , the system transfer function matrix, $\mathbf{T}$ , is given by

$$ \displaystyle\mathbf{T}(f) \displaystyle=\left[\begin{array}[]{c|cc}\mathbf{A}&\mathbf{B}_{1}&\mathbf{B}_{2}\\
\hline\cr\mathbf{C}_{1}&0&\mathbf{D}_{12}\\
\mathbf{C}_{2}&\mathbf{D}_{21}&\mathbf{D}_{22}\\
\end{array}\right] \displaystyle\equiv\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{C}_{1}\\
\mathbf{C}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\left(s-\mathbf{A}\right)^{-1}\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf{B}_{1}&\mathbf{B}_{2}\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0&\mathbf{D}_{12}\\
\mathbf{D}_{21}&\mathbf{D}_{22}\end{bmatrix}\text{.} $$

It is important to note that while the system described by $\mathbf{T}$ is often called the “plant” in controls literature, in this work it will continue to be called the system model so as to differentiate it from the plant in Fig. 1. Given a $\mathbf{T}$ in the proper form, it is possible to calculate a controller, $K$ , that minimizes the $\mathcal{H}_{2}$ norm of the combined system shown in Fig. 11 [15, 25].

The transfer function from $\vec{u}_{i}$ , restricted to only the $u_{\infty}$ , to $\vec{y}_{{}_{\text{FOM}}}$ is referred as $\mathbf{T}_{\infty}$ .*

In the following, the inputs and outputs of the $\mathbf{T}_{2}$ and $\mathbf{T}_{\infty}$ components of this system will need to be distinguished. Those can be distinguished by segmenting the noise inputs into the white noise and infinity contributions, using

and
